passages.title: A perfected Book calling to Allah alone
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat are the opening statement of Sūrah Hūd: they tell you where this Book comes from, what it was sent to say, what it asks of you, and where you are headed — **source** (ayah 1), **message** (ayah 2), **response** (ayah 3), **destination** (ayah 4).

## The surah that turned the hair of the Prophet ﷺ gray

Before a single word of the text, the sources set a mood. Abū ʿĪsā at-Tirmidhī recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās that Abū Bakr said, "O Messenger of Allah, verily your hair has turned gray." The Prophet ﷺ replied that Sūrahs Hūd, al-Wāqiʿah, al-Mursalāt, ʿAmma Yatasāʾalūn (an-Nabaʾ) and Idhā ash-Shamsu Kuwwirat (at-Takwīr) had turned his hair gray; in another narration, "Sūrah Hūd and its sisters." Maʿārif ul Qurʾān reports the same incident: when a few strands of hair in the blessed beard of the Prophet ﷺ had turned visibly gray, Abū Bakr (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu) said out of concern, "you have become old," and he ﷺ answered, "Yes, Sūrah Hūd has made me old" (reported by al-Ḥākim and Tirmidhī).

Why this surah? Because, as Maʿārif ul Qurʾān explains, Sūrah Hūd is among the surahs that describe — in a way that is unique — the coming of several kinds of mass punishments triggered by divine displeasure, as well as the terrible happenings of the fateful Day of Judgement and its outcome in individual reward and punishment. The sense of that hadith, it says, is that such was the awe and terror inspired by the mention of these happenings that it caused the emergence of the signs of old age. That is the temperature at which this surah is set.

## Alif Lām Rā

The surah opens with three isolated letters. Ibn Kathīr does not reopen the discussion here; a discussion of the letters that appear at the beginning of some chapters of the Qur'ān has already preceded at the start of Sūrat al-Baqarah, and he considers that sufficient without any need for repetition. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān states the position plainly: these are isolated letters whose meaning is a secret between Allah taʿālā and His Messenger ﷺ. Others have not been informed about it — rather, they have been prohibited from even worrying about it.

## "A Book whose verses are perfected, then set out in detail"

Everything after the letters in ayah 1 is a description of the Qur'ān itself, in two verbs.

**uḥkimat — "made firm, perfected."** The word *muḥkam* comes from *iḥkām*. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān, citing Qurṭubī, defines it as such a correct balancing of meaningful speech as would not leave the probability of any error or disorder in word or in meaning. On that definition, to say the verses have been made *muḥkam* is to say Allah taʿālā has made them such as do not admit of any likelihood or probability of error in words, or disorder in meanings, or defect, or falsity. Not "mostly reliable." Structurally airtight.

Ibn ʿAbbās (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu) read the word from a second angle, also transmitted through Qurṭubī: here *muḥkam* stands in contrast to *mansūkh*, "abrogated." Earlier Books — the Tawrāh, the Injīl — were abrogated after the revelation of the Qur'ān. But after the revelation of this Book, since the very chain of the coming of prophets and revelations came to an end, this Book will not be abrogated until the last day of Qiyāmah. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān is careful to add that the abrogation of some verses of the Qur'ān through the Qur'ān itself is not contrary to this.

**thumma fuṣṣilat — "then set out in detail."** Maʿārif ul Qurʾān opens the root: the real meaning of *tafṣīl* is to separate two things and make them distinct from each other — which is why the different sections in ordinary Arabic books bear the heading *faṣl*. Two readings follow. First, that the verses concerning beliefs, acts of worship, dealings, social living, morals and so on have been separated from each other and described clearly. Second, that as far as the will of Allah taʿālā is concerned, the entire Qur'ān had already been embedded in *al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ*, the Preserved Tablet, and was later revealed bit by bit in many installments as necessitated by different conditions prevailing among peoples and countries — so that its preservation could become easy and acting upon it functionally convenient.

Notice how the two verbs relate. Ibn Kathīr, reporting from Mujāhid and Qatādah — an interpretation Ibn Jarīr [aṭ-Ṭabarī] preferred — puts it in a single line: **perfect in its wording, detailed in its meaning; thus complete in its form and its meaning.** And the particle *thumma*, "then," matters: perfection comes first, elaboration after.

## "From One Who is All-Wise, All-Aware"

Ayah 1 closes by naming the source: *min ladun Ḥakīm Khabīr*. Ibn Kathīr: it is from Allah, Who is Most Wise in His statements and His laws, and Most Aware of the final outcome of matters.

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān draws out what those two names together mean: all these verses have come from a Sacred Being who is absolutely and simultaneously Wise and Aware. There are so many considerations of wisdom ingrained in everything that issues forth from Him that it is impossible for human beings to encompass them all. And He is fully aware of every particle of this many-sided universe, present now or to be present in the future, knowing all states of their existence as it is and as it will be, and releasing His commands keeping all of this in sight.

Then comes the contrast that makes the point land. This is not like what human beings do: no matter how intelligent, smart and experienced they may be, their reason and vision are still cordoned by a limited frame of reference, and their experience is only the product of what is around them. That, Maʿārif ul Qurʾān notes, is why human judgement mostly proves unsuccessful, even wrong, especially where it concerns what would happen in the future under different times and conditions. A command issuing from a *Ḥakīm Khabīr* is under no such limit.

## Ayah 2: what the whole Book was sent to say

Having described the Book, Allah now states its purpose: **"that you worship none but Allah."**

Ibn Kathīr's phrasing is worth holding onto: this Qur'ān descended, perfect and detailed, *with the purpose of* Allah's worship alone, without any partners. All that perfection of wording, all that careful separation of subjects — it was for this. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān says the same from the other side: from the second verse begins the delineation of one of the most important and foremost of themes, *tawḥīd*, the Oneness of Allah taʿālā — that among the things stated in these verses, the most important and foremost is that no one else should be worshipped except the One Allah.

And it is not a new message. Ibn Kathīr places it in line with two other ayat: *"And We did not send any Messenger before you but We revealed to him: there is no god but I, so worship Me"* (21:25), and *"And verily We have sent among every nation a Messenger: worship Allah alone and avoid Ṭāghūt"* (16:36) — *ṭāghūt* meaning the false deities people call upon. Every prophet carried this one sentence.

## "A warner and a bringer of glad tidings"

The second half of ayah 2 turns to the messenger: *"Surely I am to you, from Him, a warner and a bringer of good news."* Ibn Kathīr: a warner of the punishment if you oppose Allah, a bringer of the good news of reward if you obey Him. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān notes that the noble Messenger of Allah ﷺ has been commanded to tell the whole world through these verses that he is for them a carrier of warning — against disobedience — and a bearer of glad tidings of blessings in this life and in the life to come.

Do not let the word *nadhīr* harden into something cold. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān opens it beautifully: *nadhīr* is usually taken to mean a person who puts the fear of something into someone's heart — but the word is not used of a fear-generating enemy, or a beast, or anything else that harms. Instead, *nadhīr* is applied to a person who, **out of his love and affection** for someone, warns him against and saves him from things that would harm him — whether the harm is in this world or in the Hereafter. Warning, in this vocabulary, is an act of care.

Ibn Kathīr illustrates it with an authentic hadith he cites for this ayah: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ascended Mount aṣ-Ṣafā and called out to his near relatives of the Quraysh. When they gathered around him he said, "O people of Quraysh, if I informed you that a cavalry was going to attack you in the morning, would you not believe me?" They replied, "We have not found you to be a liar." He ﷺ said, "Verily I am a warner unto you before a severe punishment." That is the whole logic of *nadhīr*: a man who has never lied to you, telling you what is coming while there is still time to move.

## Ayah 3: seek forgiveness — then turn back

The second instruction comes in ayah 3: *"and that you seek forgiveness from your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān separates the two cleanly: *maghfirah*, forgiveness, relates to **past** sins; *tawbah*, repentance, relates to the **resolve not to go near them anymore**. Ibn Kathīr says the same in a single sentence — "I am commanding you to seek forgiveness from previous sins and to turn to Allah from future sins, and thereafter you abide by that." That last clause is the part people drop. In reality, as Maʿārif ul Qurʾān describes it, a correct and true tawbah is no more than three things together: being ashamed of past sins, praying to Allah that they be forgiven, and resolving firmly that they will not be repeated in future.

Which is why some righteous elders said, as Qurṭubī transmits, that seeking forgiveness from Allah only verbally — without a firm resolution and the necessary arrangements to implement it, so as to remain safe from future sins — is *tawbat al-kadhdhābīn*, the repentance of liars. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān adds a line said poetically: "Sin laughs at my style of seeking forgiveness" — or, as it puts it, such repentance is itself worth being repented. The test is not the words; the test is whether anything in your arrangements changed.

## What is promised to those who return

**"He will grant you good enjoyment for an appointed term."** Ibn Kathīr reads *mataʿan ḥasanan* as referring to this worldly life, and takes *"for a term appointed, and bestow His abounding grace to every owner of grace"* as referring to the Hereafter, according to Qatādah, comparing it to *"Whoever works righteousness — whether male or female — while a true believer, verily to him We will give a good life"* (16:97).

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān reports that most commentators have taken *mataʿan ḥasanan* to mean worldly enjoyments specifically: that as a result of the forgiveness sought and the repentance shown, Allah taʿālā blesses a person with extended sustenance and easy modalities of comfort, and protects him from calamities and punishments. Its supporting evidence is Sūrah Nūḥ, where the address is to the seekers of forgiveness: *"He will send the sky showering over you, and bless you with wealth and children, and make for you gardens and bring for you rivers"* (71:11–12) — rain, wealth, children, gardens: obviously blessings of the life of this present world. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān also notes that according to the investigations of the majority of commentators, the "good life" of 16:97 includes **both** the life of this world and the life of the Hereafter.

And then the honest caveat: *ilā ajalin musamman*, "for a given time." Since this worldly life must end some day, the enjoyment of its comforts cannot become eternal; by adding this caveat it has been stressed that the good things to enjoy in the present world will be available up to a particular time — the time of death. On the final count, death will eliminate all of these things. But, Maʿārif ul Qurʾān adds, soon after that death the life of the other world will begin, and there too eternal comforts will be available to those who repent and seek forgiveness.

There is also a quieter reading of "good things to enjoy." Sahl ibn ʿAbdullāh (raḥimahullāh) said its meaning is that one's attention bypasses the created and remains fixed on the Creator. Some other men of Allah said its reality is that one remains content with what is available and worries not for what is not — satisfied with as much as is within easy reach in this world, not eating his heart out for what he does not have. On that reading, the reward for repentance is not a larger pile; it is a heart that has stopped grasping.

**"And bestow His grace on every possessor of grace."** Maʿārif ul Qurʾān unpacks the two occurrences of *faḍl*: the first refers to one's own good deed, the second denotes divine grace and bounty, that is, Paradise. Put simply, Allah taʿālā shall bless every doer of a good deed with His grace, Paradise. So ayah 3 has now made a promise of a good life in both this world and the Hereafter, and then of the everlasting blessings of Paradise.

## "But if you turn away"

Only after all of that does the warning come: *"And if you turn away, then I fear for you the punishment of a great Day."* Ibn Kathīr calls this a severe threat for whoever turns away from the commandments of Allah, the Exalted, and rejects His Messengers — the punishment will afflict such a person on the Day of Resurrection and there will be no escape from it. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān spells out what "turning away" means concretely: to turn away from the good counsel just given, to fail to seek forgiveness for past sins, and to fail to remain safe against sins in the future. The Day is called *kabīr*, "great," it explains, because it would be a day of a thousand years, and also because, in terms of what would transpire in it, it will be the gravest.

Note the wording the Messenger ﷺ is given: not "you will be punished," but *"I fear for you."* Even the warning is delivered in the voice of someone frightened on your behalf — which is exactly the *nadhīr* of ayah 2, one who warns out of love and affection.

## Ayah 4: "To Allah is your return"

The passage closes by removing the last exit. *"To Allah is your return"* — Ibn Kathīr: your return on the Day of Judgement. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān sets it against human bravado: let a man do what he elects to do, let him live the way he fancies — but ultimately, once dead, he has to return to Him.

*"And He is able to do all things."* Ibn Kathīr explains this as His being capable of doing whatever He wishes, whether it be goodness towards His awliyāʾ — His friends and allies — or vengeance upon His enemies; and this also includes His ability to repeat the creation of His creatures on the Day of Resurrection. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān presses exactly there: it is not at all difficult for Him to have each particle a man is made of reassembled after he is dead and has become dust, and to see to it that the same man rises all over again.

And Ibn Kathīr closes the passage with a remark that captures its architecture: **this section encourages fear, just as the previous section encourages hope.** Ayah 3 held out good provision, a good life and Paradise; ayah 4 holds out an inescapable return to One who is able to do all things. Hope and fear, set side by side.

## Living it

- **Take the Book as *muḥkam*.** Nothing came after it to abrogate it, and nothing will until the last day of Qiyāmah. What it asks of you today it will still be asking then.
- **Let the purpose govern the reading.** Ibn Kathīr says the Qur'ān descended perfect and detailed *with the purpose of* the worship of Allah alone, without any partners. If study is not producing worship, it has missed the stated point.
- **Do istighfār and tawbah as two acts, not one phrase.** Ask forgiveness for what is behind you; then make an actual firm resolution about what is ahead, and put the necessary arrangements in place to implement it. Words without that, the righteous elders said, are the repentance of liars.
- **Expect the reward in both worlds, and hold the worldly half loosely.** It is real — extended sustenance, ease, protection — but it is stamped *ilā ajalin musamman*, up to the time of death. What is not stamped is what begins soon after.

passages.title: Nothing is hidden from the Sustainer of all
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These four ayat set one small, futile human gesture — folding yourself up so as not to be seen — against the immensity of the One it is aimed at. That is the thread through ayat 5–8: nothing is hidden from the Sustainer of all — not what is folded inside a chest, not a creature's whereabouts, not the hour of a punishment the mockers keep demanding.

## Ayah 5 — folding the chest against the Knower of what is in chests

Ibn Kathir renders the ayah: *"No doubt! They did fold up their breasts, that they may hide from Him. Surely, even when they cover themselves with their garments, He knows what they conceal and what they reveal. Verily, He is the All-Knower of the (innermost secrets) of the breasts."*

**Reports from Ibn ʿAbbas.** al-Bukhari recorded — by way of Ibn Jurayj, who reported from Muhammad bin ʿAbbad bin Jaʿfar — that Ibn ʿAbbas recited the words as *tathnawnī ṣudūruhum*, and when he was asked what "their breasts did fold up" means, he answered: "The man used to have sex with his woman, but he would be shy, or he used to have answering the call of nature (in an open space) but, he would be shy. Therefore, this verse… was revealed."

And in a further report, al-Bukhari records Ibn ʿAbbas explaining *yastaghshūn* — "they cover themselves" — as meaning **that they cover their heads**. On this reading the ayah addresses an instinct rather than exposing a plot: the shyness is real, but a garment pulled over the head does not put a person outside Allah's knowledge.

**The reading in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān.** There the ayah carries a refutation of the hypocrites and the disbelievers, who "try to camouflage their hostility, and their antagonistic activism against the Holy Prophet ﷺ as deftly as they could… and surmise that no one would find out who they were really." But the truth, says Maʿārif, is that Allah knows it all — what they let come out in the open and what they conceal "behind all sorts of clothes, covers and curtains" — because إِنَّهُ عَلِيمٌ بِذَاتِ الصُّدُورِ, "He is All Aware of [even] what lies in the hearts."

A person may fold his body, cover his head, and manage his face perfectly; the layer that matters is not a layer to Allah at all.

## Ayah 6 — from concealment to provision

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān shows the joint. In consonance with "the all-encompassing knowledge of Allah Taʿala from whom nothing is hidden," this ayah mentions a great favour: Allah has Himself taken the responsibility of providing sustenance. So, Maʿārif concludes, "the intentions and efforts of disbelievers and hypocrites to hide things from Allah Taʿala are nothing but ignorance and senselessness."

**How wide is the net?** *Dābbah* is any creature that moves on earth. Maʿārif notes that to intensify this generality the word مِن (*min*) has been added — *wa mā min dābbatin*. It includes "all beasts, birds, insects and all animals of the land and the sea," birds because their nests too are located somewhere on the land. Ibn Kathir says the same: Allah is responsible for the provisions of all creatures that dwell in the earth, "whether they are small, large, sea-dwelling or land-dwelling."

**"…whose provision is upon Allah."** The Arabic is عَلَى اللَّهِ رِزْقُهَا — *its sustenance is on Allah*. Maʿārif notes this is worded in a way "which give[s] the impression of a duty imposed on someone." Yet "it is obvious that there is no power that could put a liability on Allah Taʿala." The word is there because "Allah Taʿala himself has made this promise out of his grace and mercy," and the promise comes from One who is True and Merciful: "There is no probability of things happening otherwise, counter to the promise. This is a matter of certitude."

**What *rizq* means.** Maʿārif defines it lexically as "something from which a creature procures its food and through which the body grows and the soul survives." First, having rizq does not imply owning it — rizq is given to all animals, but they are not its owners and "are not cut out for ownership." Second, the ʿUlamaʼ have said that in this general sense rizq could be halal (lawful) and could also be haram (unlawful), "because for a person who eats up what belongs to the other person, that property, no doubt, becomes his food, but so it becomes only unlawfully." And Maʿārif adds the sting: "Had this person not used unfair means blinded by his greed, he would have received the halal rizq reserved and appointed for him."

**"He knows its dwelling place and its deposit."** ʿAli bin Abi Talhah and others reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that *mustaqarr* means where the creature resides, and *mustawdaʿ* **where it will die**. Ibn Kathir glosses the pair as Allah's knowing "where their journeying will end in the earth and where they will seek shelter when they wish to nest." Maʿārif observes that lexically what Tafsir al-Kashshaf carries is the closest: *mustaqarr* is the place someone makes a permanent residence or home, and *mustawdaʿ* a place where one stays temporarily to take care of something.

Maʿārif turns this into an image. Suppose some person or institution took responsibility for delivering your provision. If you travelled, you would have to notify them, and "give a firm itinerary that you will be living in such and such city or village, from such and such date to such and such date." But when the matter is *ʿalā Allah*, "you do not have to take even this much of trouble because He knows when you move and He knows when you do not… He needs no application, or advice or address to take care of your rizq. It is just delivered wherever you are."

**But people do starve.** Maʿārif raises the objection: when Allah has taken responsibility for the food of every creature, why do many animals and human beings die of hunger and thirst? One answer of the ʿUlamaʼ is that the responsibility of rizq is there **until the appointed time comes** — until the end of the years of life. When those years are over one has to die; and it could be that the rizq of the person concerned was stopped, and that is what caused death.

**The Ashʿari emissary.** Imam al-Qurtubi mentions an event related to Abu Musa, Abu Malik and some others of their tribe of Banu al-Ashʿar, as Maʿārif relates it. When they reached Madinah after their Hijrah, the wherewithal of their journey was all used up. They sent one of their men to the Prophet ﷺ hoping he would arrange their meals. When the man reached his door, he heard the Prophet ﷺ reciting this very ayah — *and there is no creature on earth whose sustenance is not on Allah*. Hearing it, he thought: we Ashʿarites too would not be any worse than the animals in the sight of Allah; He shall most certainly give us our rizq. With that thought he turned from the door and left. Back with his tribe he said, "Rejoice, my friends. The help of Allah is coming for you." Hardly had they sat down when two men arrived carrying a trencher full of meat and bread. The Ashʿarites ate their fill, and as food was still left, they sent the rest to the Prophet ﷺ. Later they came to him and said, "Ya Rasulallah, the food you sent was very nice and very delicious." He said, "As for me, I never sent any food" — it was sent by the Most Sacred Being who has taken the responsibility of providing rizq to every living creature.

**Musa and the creature in the rock.** Maʿārif also relates, on the authority of some hadith reports, that when Sayyidna Musa (peace be upon him) was made a prophet at the Mount of Tur and told to go to Egypt, it occurred to him that he had left his wife alone in a wilderness — who would take care of her? To remove this scruple from his heart, Allah told him to strike his rod at the rock in front of him. The rock split, and out came another; he struck that too, and out came a third; striking that, he saw coming out of it a creature holding a green leaf in its mouth. Musa (peace be upon him) had believed in the perfect power of Allah before this, "but what one sees with one's eyes has an effect of its own." So he set off for Egypt from that very spot.

**"All is in a clear Book."** Ibn Kathir notes that Allah informs us all of this is written in a Book with Him that explains it in detail, and links the ayah to *"There is not a moving creature on earth, nor a bird that flies with its two wings, but are communities like you. We have neglected nothing in the Book"* (6:38), and to *"not a leaf falls, but He knows it… nor anything fresh or dry, but is written in a Clear Record"* (6:59).

Maʿārif asks why a record is mentioned at all: His will alone would have been sufficient to make everything come out right, "without the need to maintain a log book or master file of work done." But the only analogy weak man has is the analogy of the system he is used to, and so "he could have apprehensions of possible errors and omissions." This clear Book, Maʿārif explains, means al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ, the Preserved Tablet, with universal coverage and full details of sustenance, age, deeds and the like, entrusted to the angels concerned as and when needed.

Two hadith are cited. As narrated by Sayyidna ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) and reported in the Sahih of Muslim, the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah had written the destinies of all His creation fifty thousand years even before the creation of the heavens and the earth. And a lengthy hadith narrated by Sayyidna ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud (may Allah be pleased with him), appearing in al-Bukhari and Muslim, reports the Prophet ﷺ saying — in Maʿārif's summary — that man passes through stages before birth, and when the parts of his body are formed completely, Allah commands an angel who writes down four things about him: the deeds he will do; his years of life, with even the month, day, minute and breath count recorded; where he will die and where he will be buried; and his rizq — how much it is, and how and where it has to reach him.

## Ayah 7 — the Throne over the water, and why any of this exists

*He created the heavens and the earth in six Days, and His Throne was over the water.* Ibn Kathir says Allah here informs of His power over all things.

**From the Sunnah.** Imam Ahmad recorded that ʿImran bin Husayn said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ told the tribe of Tamim to accept glad tidings, and then said the same to the people of Yemen. They said, "We accept. Therefore, inform us about the beginning of this matter and how it was." He ﷺ said: **"Allah was before everything and His Throne was over the water. He then wrote in the Preserved Tablet mentioning everything."** Ibn Kathir notes that this hadith has been recorded in the Two Sahihs of al-Bukhari and Muslim with a variety of wordings.

In Sahih Muslim it is recorded that ʿAbdullah bin ʿAmr bin al-ʿAs said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Verily Allah measured the amount of sustenance of the creatures fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth, and His Throne was over the water."

And under the explanation of this verse, al-Bukhari recorded from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah, the Mighty and Sublime, said, 'Spend and I will spend on you.'" And he ﷺ said, "Allah's Hand is full, and it is not diminished by spending throughout the night and the day." And he ﷺ also said, "Have you seen what has been spent since the creation of the heavens and the earth? Verily it does not diminish what is in His Right Hand (in the slightest) — and His Throne was over the water. In His Hand is the Scale and He lowers and raises it."

**The six Days.** Maʿārif notes that this ayah tells us water was created before the heavens and the earth, and that the elaboration of the six days appears in Surah Ha Mim as-Sajdah (Surah Fussilat): the earth in two days; mountains, river streams, trees and the means of sustenance and survival for living creatures in two days; then the seven heavens in two days (41:9–12). According to Tafsir Mazhari, a day is the measure of time which — *after* the creation of the heavens and the earth — is from sunrise to sunset, although at the time of that creation neither did the sun exist nor its rising and setting. Maʿārif adds that it was within the perfect power of Allah to create all this in the flash of a moment, but in His wisdom He has made the system of this world gradual, suitable for human temperament.

**The stated purpose: "that He might try you, which of you is best in deeds."** Ibn Kathir: this means He created the heavens and the earth for the benefit of His servants; Allah did not create this creation out of mere frivolity — as in *"And We created not the heaven and the earth and all that is between them without purpose"* (38:27), *"Did you think that We created you in play?"* (23:115–116), and *"And I created not the Jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me"* (51:56).

Maʿārif reaches the same conclusion: they were created for human beings, and "it is expected of them that they would ponder over these and would not miss to recognize their Master and Lord." Maʿārif adds, citing Mazhari, that since among the progeny of Sayyidna Adam (peace be upon him) the best in deeds is our Rasul ﷺ, it is correct to say that the real purpose of creating the entire universe is to bless it with his generous presence, serving as a model right through the Last Day.

**Best, not most.** Ibn Kathir: "It is important to note here that Allah did not say, 'Which of you has done the most deeds.' Rather, He said, 'Best in deeds.'" And he states the standard plainly — a deed cannot be considered a good deed until it is done sincerely for Allah, and it must be in accordance with the legislation of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; whenever a deed lacks one of these conditions, it is null and void. Maʿārif draws the same lesson: Allah favours the quality of a deed more than the abundance of good deeds such as Salah, Sawm, recitation of the Qurʼan and dhikr. This excellence is expressed in hadith by the word *iḥsān*. "In a nutshell," says Maʿārif, "a little done with total sincerity and according to Sunnah is better than a lot more done with none, or less of the two."

## Ayat 7b–8 — "obvious magic," and "what is keeping it back?"

Tell them they will be raised after death, and those who disbelieve are sure to say: *this is nothing but obvious magic.* Ibn Kathir points out the incoherence. These are people who, if asked who created them, would surely say "Allah" (43:87); if asked who created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon, would surely reply "Allah" (29:61). Yet in reference to ability, the resurrection is easier for Allah to perform than the original creation: *"He it is Who originates the creation, then He will repeat it; and this is easier for Him"* (30:27), and *"The creation of you all and the resurrection of you all are only as (the creation and resurrection of) a single person"* (31:28). Their "obvious magic," says Ibn Kathir, is said out of disbelief and obstinacy; part of their claim was that he ﷺ says this only because he is bewitched. Maʿārif reads it as the reflex of chronic deniers: what they do not understand — or do not want to — they dismiss as magic.

**The word *ummah*.** Ayah 8 speaks of delaying the punishment *ilā ummatin maʿdūdah*, and Ibn Kathir notes that here it does not mean a community. Among its senses in the Qurʼan and Sunnah are: the Imam or leader who is followed — "Verily, Ibrahim was an *Ummah*, obedient to Allah" (16:120); religion and religious creed (43:23); a group of people (28:23), including those among whom a Messenger was sent (16:36; 10:47); the Ummah of followers who believe in the Messengers (3:110); and a sect or party (7:159; 3:113). But it is also used to mean **a specified period of time** — as with the released prisoner in Surah Yusuf who "after an *Ummah* remembered" (12:45) — and that, says Ibn Kathir, is the sense here: until a determined, counted term.

**Their demand.** Ibn Kathir renders the sense: if We delay the torment of these polytheists until an appointed and specific time period, they would still say, in rejection and haste, "What keeps it back?" Maʿārif reads ayah 8 as the answer given to people who doubted the warnings of punishment given by the prophets (peace be on them) and asked why the punishment they warned of would not come.

The ayah answers in its own terms: **on the day it reaches them, nothing will turn it away from them, and they will be surrounded by that at which they used to mock.** Ibn Kathir: both rejection and doubt are their very nature; therefore, they have no escape or refuge from the torment. A delay is not an acquittal; it is a counted term running out.

## Living with these ayat

**Stop performing** (ayah 5): whatever you fold away from people is open to the One who is All Aware of what lies in the hearts, so the honest work is inside, not on the covering. **Let the guarantee change your anxiety, not your ethics** (ayah 6): the promise of provision needs no application or address from you — but rizq can also be taken unlawfully. **Aim at quality** (ayah 7): the purpose of the whole creation is a test of *best*, not *most* — a little with sincerity and Sunnah over a great deal without. And **distrust the mocker's arithmetic** (ayah 8): that the punishment has not yet arrived proves nothing, except that the term is counted — and counted terms end.

passages.title: Human ingratitude in ease and hardship
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat turn the light onto the human heart itself: how a person behaves when a blessing is taken away, and how he behaves when relief arrives after hardship. Two mirror-image reversals in ayat 9 and 10 — and then, in ayah 11, the single exception that rescues a person from both.

**Where this sits in the surah.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out the placement. The verses just before these had confirmed that the Prophet ﷺ is a Messenger of Allah and answered those who "engineer doubts" about it. Now, at the head of what follows, an instinctively bad human habit is named — and it is named, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, "with an instruction to Muslims that they should stay away from it." So this is not only a description of how other people fail. It is a diagnosis of a weakness in human temperament that Muslims are being told to keep clear of.

## The two reversals

In ayah 9, Allah speaks of giving a person a taste of mercy — and the ayah names the source, `مِنَّا`, *from Us* — and then withdrawing it, so that the person turns "despairing, ungrateful."

Ibn Kathir unpacks what that despair actually does to a man's memory: when hardship befalls him *after* he has known blessing, "he is disheartened and he despairs of any good in the future. He denies and rejects (the bounties of) his previous condition. Thus, he behaves as if he has never seen any good and he loses all hope for relief."

Notice how much is wrong in that one movement of the heart. He loses the future (no good is coming). He erases the past (he acts as though he had never been given anything). And, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds with great force: "He never thinks that Allah who blessed him first could bless him again." The very hand that gave once is still there — but a man consumed by his present moment cannot see past it.

Ayah 10 turns the picture over. Give the same man ease after hardship has touched him — the "evil" of this ayah is rendered in Ibn Kathir's text as "poverty and harm" — and he says, `لَيَقُولَنَّ ذَهَبَ السَّيِّئَاتُ عَنِّي`, "Ills have departed from me." Ibn Kathir's comment is precise and slightly chilling: "This means that he will claim that no harm or calamity will afflict him after this (blessing)." It is not gratitude for relief. It is a verdict that suffering is now behind him for good.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the same failure of memory in the opposite direction. Rather than recalling his past suffering, turning to Allah and being grateful to Him, the man "starts waxing more proud and arrogant." He forgets his past, comes to think that Allah's blessings were his right, that he has to have them, and that this is how life will run for the rest of his days. And here is the blindness at the centre of it: "it just does not occur to him that the way the days of suffering did not continue any more, the same thing could happen to the days of comfort and they too could vanish."

The two ayat, read together, expose one single flaw wearing two faces. In hardship he cannot believe good will return; in ease he cannot believe hardship will. Both come from the same place — what Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls the "worship of the present."

## Why the Qur'an says "a taste"

The verb in these ayat is `أَذَقْنَا` — *We gave him a taste*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes this the interpretive key to the whole passage: the Qur'an "uses the word: اَذَقنَا (adhaqna: We give them a taste of) for blessing and suffering both," and "by this device, it was indicated that real blessing and suffering is that of the Hereafter."

Neither the comfort of this world nor its suffering is the whole of it. Each is at the level of tasting and sampling, so that human beings can have some idea of the blessings and sufferings of the Hereafter. From which follows the conclusion Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states plainly: "neither are the comforts of this world something to be happy about unnecessarily, nor are its sufferings something to grieve about too much." The image it leaves you with is memorable — this whole world is, to borrow a commercial term, "only a showroom of the Hereafter with sample displays of comfort and suffering."

A man who understands that he is standing in a showroom does not stake his hope or his despair on the samples.

## "Exultant and boastful"

Ayah 10 ends with two words: `إِنَّهُ لَفَرِحٌ فَخُورٌ` — "he is exultant and boastful." Ibn Kathir glosses the phrase in a single stroke: "This means that he is pleased with what he has in his hand and ungrateful (to Allah). At the same time he is boastful towards others."

So the failure points in two directions at once. Upward, toward Allah: he is delighted with the gift in his hand and gives no thanks to the Giver. Sideways, toward other human beings: the gift becomes a way of standing above them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes this to its ugliest form. So tragic is the human penchant for forgetting, it says, that "a power-hungry man would not even blink to raise the edifice of his power on the blood and dust of another man of power. Always looking up, he would never look down to recall that this had been the fate of the man of power before him. Sad ends and ill fates make no effect on him for power in the present tastes good."

And this, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, is precisely the moment revelation is needed. "When people start worshipping the present and elect to remain drunk with the state they are in, that is high time for Books of Allah and His Messengers to come." What they bring is perspective: they bring "the lesson-oriented events of the past into sharp focus for heedless man to see things in this perspective and have a little concern for what would happen to them in the future." The lesson they teach, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's words: ponder over the changing conditions of the universe you are in and get to know the Power working behind them.

## The exception: ayah 11

`إِلَّا الَّذِينَ صَبَرُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ` — "except those who are patient and do good deeds." Ibn Kathir had already framed the whole passage this way: Allah is informing about "mankind and the blameworthy characteristics that he possesses, *except for those believing servants upon whom Allah has bestowed His mercy*." In Ibn Kathir's wording, the exception is tied to a mercy Allah has bestowed.

**Sabr is stronger than "patience."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān warns that the English word is too narrow — *ṣabr* carries "a much wider range of meanings in the Arabic language, much wider than conveyed by its translation as 'patience' in English." Its real meaning is "to tie, check, stop or hold back," and in the terminology of the Qur'an and Sunnah it is holding the desiring human self back from what is impermissible. So *ṣabr* here is not merely enduring a bad month with a set jaw. It includes, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's words, "abstention from all sins and doings counter to the dictates of the Sharīʿah." It is restraint of the self, not just tolerance of circumstance.

Its partner, *al-ʿamal aṣ-ṣāliḥ* (good deeds), Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says "covers all that is obligatory (fard), necessary (wajib), Sunnah and recommended (mustahabb)." Between the two, the believer's life is accounted for — he abstains from everything disliked by Allah and His Rasūl and races towards every deed that brings their pleasure. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names what makes this possible: faith in Allah, and fear of the reckoning of the Last Day of Qiyāmah. A man who is answerable to a coming Day is not owned by his present one.

**Each quality has its season.** This is the elegance of ayah 11 as Ibn Kathir reads it. "Except those who show patience" means "those who show patience during times of hardship and adversity." "And do righteous good deeds" means "they perform the good deeds in times of ease and good health." Hardship is met with *ṣabr* instead of despair; ease is met with obedience instead of boasting — which is to say, the two states of ayat 9 and 10 each have their own act of worship waiting inside them. Nothing in a believer's life is wasted.

**The reward is mapped just as carefully.** Ibn Kathir reads the closing phrases against the same two states. "Those, theirs will be forgiveness" — "meaning, that they will be forgiven due to the calamities that afflicted them." "And a great reward" — "this great reward is due to them because of what they sent forth (of good deeds) in their times of ease."

Read that slowly. The very hardship that made the other man despair is, for this man, the thing his sins are washed away by. The very ease in which the other man boasted is, for this man, the capital he sent forward. Two people can live through the same two seasons and walk out of them into completely different destinations.

## From the Sunnah

After the phrase about the great reward, Ibn Kathir says this is similar to what is mentioned in the Hadith: by the One in whose Hand is my soul, no worry, calamity, distress, illness, or grief strikes a believer, even the prick of a thorn, except that Allah will expiate his sins for him because of it. (Ibn Kathir cites this without naming a collection, so it is left unnamed here too.)

Then, "In the Sahih it is recorded," he says, that the Prophet ﷺ said: by the One in whose Hand is my soul, Allah does not decree any matter for the believer except that it is good for him — if any blessing befalls him, he is thankful and that is good for him; if any harm comes to him, he is patient and that too is good for him; and this is a bounty exclusively for the believer.

That last clause is the passage in miniature. The hadith names the same two situations the ayat have been describing — `سَرَّاءُ` (blessing) and `ضَرَّاءُ` (harm), the very word ayah 10 uses for the hardship that touched the man. What decides the outcome is not which of the two you are handed. It is thankfulness in the one and patience in the other. And that double profit, the hadith says, belongs to nobody but the believer.

## Man as he is, left to himself

To show that this is a settled Qur'anic verdict and not a passing remark, Ibn Kathir links these ayat to two other places. Sūrat al-ʿAsr: by time — man is in loss, "except those who believe and do righteous good deeds. And recommend one another to the truth and recommend one another to patience" (103:1–3). The same structure exactly: a sweeping statement about humanity, then a narrow exception built out of faith, righteous deeds, and patience. And 70:19, "Verily, man was created very impatient."

The Qur'an is not flattering us and it is not despairing of us. It is telling us what the raw material is, so that we know what has to be worked on.

## Living it

**When a blessing is withdrawn, refuse the two lies.** The first is that no good is coming; the second is that no good ever came. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's line is the cure for both: Allah who blessed you first could bless you again. Deliberately recalling His past gifts is not nostalgia — it is the antidote to despair.

**When relief arrives, do not announce that the ills are gone.** That sentence in ayah 10 is the mark of a heedless man, who claims, in Ibn Kathir's words, "that no harm or calamity will afflict him after this." The believer's response to relief is to recall what he was rescued from, turn to Allah and thank Him, and stay aware that comfort is as capable of ending as suffering was.

**Work in your good seasons.** Ibn Kathir's reading of "righteous good deeds" as deeds performed "in times of ease and good health" is quietly demanding. Health, money, free time and calm are not rewards to be enjoyed and reported; they are the window in which you send something ahead. The great reward, he says, "is due to them because of what they sent forth (of good deeds) in their times of ease."

**Look past the causes to the Causer.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's closing portrait is worth keeping: "a perfect believer, in fact, a perfect human being is one who is able to perceive the hidden Power behind every change, revolution, sorrow and comfort, ignore their transitory phases, dismiss their material causes as the sole explanation. The mark of an intelligent person is that he looks at the originator or causer of causes more than he would look at causes, and it is with Him alone that he would relate to as firmly as possible."

That is the whole passage in one sentence. The despairing man and the boasting man are both staring at their circumstances. The believer is looking at Allah.

passages.title: The Prophet's burden and the ten-sūrah challenge
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat are Allah's consolation to His Messenger ﷺ under the weight of Makkan mockery — and then His turning on the mockers with a challenge they could never meet. Ayah 12 addresses the Prophet's ﷺ heart; ayah 13 answers the accusation behind their taunts; ayah 14 draws the conclusion. What holds them together is one movement: *you are not obliged to satisfy them — and here is the proof that will silence them.*

## The moment behind ayah 12

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that ayah 12 was revealed about a particular event. The idolaters of Makkah had placed a host of demands before the Prophet ﷺ. One was about the Qur'an itself: *our idols have been maligned in this Qur'an, so we cannot believe in it — bring some other Qur'an, or improve it by making alterations in it.* Maʿārif cites this as the same demand recorded elsewhere in the Qur'an: "Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it" (Yūnus 10:15). Maʿārif attributes the account to al-Baghawī and Mazharī.

Another demand: *we will believe in your prophethood only when some treasure — like the treasures of the kings of the world — is sent down to you and you dole it out to everyone around. Or when some angel descends from the heavens and stays with you everywhere, testifying that you really are a Messenger of Allah.*

Ibn Kathir sets the same taunts alongside their parallel in Sūrat al-Furqān: "And they say: 'Why does this Messenger eat food, and walk about in the markets. Why is not an angel sent down to him to be a warner with him.' Or: '(why) has not a treasure been granted to him, or why has he not a garden whereof he may eat.' And the wrongdoers say: 'You follow none but a man bewitched'" (25:7–8).

**Why this wounded him.** Maʿārif is careful here, and the point is moving. The Prophet ﷺ felt the pinch of these absurd, even disrespectfully audacious demands in his heart — and the reason given is that *he was mercy for all the worlds*. It was not possible for him to leave them to their fate and take out of his heart the hope that they might someday believe. Nor was it possible for him to fulfil demands like theirs. So he was caught: unable to give up on them, unable to give them what they asked. That is the pressure ayah 12 speaks into.

## "So perchance you may give up a part of what is revealed unto you"

That is the rendering carried in the Ibn Kathir material, which continues: "and that your breast feels straitened for it because they say, 'Why has not a treasure been sent down unto him, or an angel come with him.' But you are only a warner. And Allah is a Guardian over all things."

Ibn Kathir explains the sense: that the Prophet ﷺ may be compelled to give up the Message because of what the polytheists were saying about him. And *wa-ḍāʼiqun bihi ṣadruk* — "your breast feels straitened for it," the chest constricted, squeezed narrow. Ibn Kathir brings the ayah that names this state openly: "Indeed, We know that your breast is straitened at what they say" (15:97). This is not an accusation; it is Allah telling His Messenger ﷺ that the tightness in his chest is fully seen and fully known. Ibn Kathir's framing of the whole passage is exactly this — that Allah's statement here *comforted* the worries the polytheists were causing him.

**The force of *laʿallaka*.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the opening word — *fa-laʿallaka*, which it glosses as "is it then expected of you...?" This does not mean that such a thing could actually be expected of him. The purpose of the phrasing is the opposite: to establish that he was free of it. He would not leave out any part of the Qur'an in consideration of their insistence — not even the part that speaks of the utter helplessness of the idols, which was exactly the part they wanted removed — nor did he have to be sad, concerned and straitened over their demands. The question is asked so that the answer, *no, never*, rings out from the Prophet's ﷺ own heart.

**Why their demands were incoherent.** Maʿārif takes them apart one by one:

- *Change the Qur'an so it stops maligning our idols.* These demands were "based on bland irrationality." If idols, idol-worship and things like that are not called what they are, what would become of right guidance and how would it be done? Guidance that cannot name falsehood is not guidance.
- *Send down a treasure.* This was a loud mismatch with the mission of a prophet. They had simply taken the station of a prophet on the analogy of the status of a king — as though prophethood were a throne with a treasury attached.
- *Attach an angel to him as a visible witness.* It is not the practice of Allah that He would create conditions under which people are materially compelled to start professing the faith. The whole world is within His power and control — who could dare profess a belief, and act on it, against His will? But in His infinite wisdom He has made this world a place of test. No material means are used here to compel people into good or out of evil. What is used is Scriptures and Apostles: lines drawn between virtue and vice, the outcome of each explained, people invited and exhorted.

Maʿārif adds a further consequence of the angel demand: had an angel been miraculously attached to a prophet to attest to the truth of his word, it would have posed problems — when someone refused to believe, he would have faced punishment on the spot. That would have been a way of compelling people to believe. Belief extracted that way would no longer be *believing without seeing*, which Maʿārif calls the very essence of belief and faith — nor would any choice be left for a person to make, which is the essence of his deed.

**What the demands revealed about them.** Maʿārif makes an observation that reframes the whole exchange: the very act of making such demands proved that these people were grossly unaware of the status and reality of a messenger and prophet of Allah. They saw no difference between Allah and His Messenger. They even took the messenger to be absolutely powerful like Allah, and so demanded of him what could not be done by anyone other than Allah. On Maʿārif's reading, then, the taunt exposed the ignorance of the ones making it more than it troubled the one it was aimed at.

## "But you are only a warner. And Allah is a Guardian over all things"

Ibn Kathir: Allah commanded His Messenger and guided him not to let these statements of theirs grieve his heart, and not to let them prevent him or deter him from calling people to Allah, both day and night. And then the consolation that carries the whole passage, in the words Ibn Kathir brings: "You are only a warner and you have an example in your brothers of the Messengers who came before you. For verily, the previous Messengers were rejected and harmed, yet they were patient until the help of Allah came to them." He is being placed in a line of brothers who were treated exactly this way and outlasted it.

**Why *nadhīr* (warner) specifically?** Maʿārif explains that *nadhīr* is mentioned here particularly because those being addressed were disbelievers, and such people deserve nothing but warning against the consequences of their deeds. Otherwise the Prophet ﷺ is not simply *nadhīr*, one who warns; he is *bashīr* too, one who announces glad tidings for people who do good deeds. And Maʿārif adds a beautiful qualification: in reality, a *nadhīr* is a person who warns *out of love and affection* against what is evil and harmful. So in a way the sense of *bashīr* is already included in the sense of *nadhīr*. A warning from someone who loves you carries good news inside it.

**"And Allah is a Guardian over all things."** This is where the burden is set down. Maʿārif states the logic plainly: he has been sent from Allah as *nadhīr* — and Allah takes care of the rest, for He is powerful over everything. The Prophet's ﷺ responsibility is the delivery. The results are not his to carry.

## Ayah 13: the challenge of ten sūrahs

The rendering carried in the Ibn Kathir material reads: "Or they say, 'He forged it.' Say: 'Bring you then ten forged Surahs like unto it, and call whomsoever you can, other than Allah, if you speak the truth!'"

Maʿārif frames the transition: in the preceding ayat the idolaters had demanded the kind of miracles *they* chose. The ayat that follow tell them they already have a miracle — the miracle of the Qur'an, shown at the hands of the Prophet ﷺ before them, a miracle even they could not deny. If they were demanding miracles honestly, only to determine the truthfulness of a messenger of Allah, then their demand already stands accepted and the miracle is on. And if the demand was simply to gratify their hostility, then showing further miracles would remain redundant — for who could expect from such hostile people that they would embrace Islam even after having seen them? The essential point stands: the Qur'an is a clear miracle that cannot be denied.

**Notice how the challenge is built.** Maʿārif: if you really think Muhammad ﷺ can make a Qur'an like this all by himself, then you too, better come up with only ten sūrahs like it. And it is not necessary either that these ten be the work of any one person — let everyone in the world join forces and come up with them. The ayah opens the door as wide as it goes: *call whomsoever you can, other than Allah.*

**And notice what kind of sūrahs are asked for.** The wording is "ten *forged* Surahs like unto it." The challenge concedes their own premise: make them up, exactly as you claim he made his up. They are not asked to produce genuine revelation — only something *like it*. The bar is set as low as it can be set, and it is still out of reach.

## Why the Qur'an cannot be matched

Ibn Kathir gives the reason: no one is able to produce its like, or even bring ten chapters, or one chapter like it — **because the Speech of the Lord of all that exists is not like the speech of the created beings, just as His attributes are not like the attributes of the creation. Nothing resembles His existence.** Exalted is He, the Most Holy and the Sublime. There is no deity worthy of worship except He, and there is no true Lord other than He.

Notice where Ibn Kathir locates the reason. He does not rest the Qur'an's inimitability on the literary limits of any particular audience. He rests it on the difference between the Speech of the Lord and the speech of creation — and, alongside that, he states that Allah's attributes are not like the attributes of creation and that nothing resembles His existence. Human speech can be matched by human speech. This cannot be matched, because it did not come from that side of the divide.

Maʿārif adds the historical sequel: they were first asked to bring ten sūrahs, and they failed to do so. Then, to make their inability look more pronounced, the challenge was reduced in another ayah — "Then, bring a sūrah the like of this" (al-Baqarah 2:23). If you take the Qur'an to be the word of man, bring no more than just one sūrah like it. Despite the challenge being made that easy for them, they could do nothing. It stood proved, Maʿārif concludes, that the Qur'an was a miracle and the Word of Allah without any doubt.

## Ayah 14: what their silence proves

The rendering carried in the Ibn Kathir material reads: "If then they answer you not, know then that it is sent down with the knowledge of Allah and that there is no god besides Him! Will you then be Muslims?"

Ibn Kathir: if they do not come with a reply to that which you have challenged them with — the reproduction of ten chapters like the Qur'an — then know that it is due to their *inability* to do so. Know that this is a proof: that this is the speech revealed from Allah, containing His knowledge, His commands and His prohibitions. Maʿārif puts the same argument the other way round: had this Qur'an been the word of some human being, other human beings would also have been able to make something like it. That all of them fail to do so is a strong proof that this Qur'an was revealed only with the knowledge of Allah — knowledge in which there is no room for the least increase or decrease — and that it is beyond human power.

**A note on the opening clause.** The Arabic of ayah 14 addresses a plural "you" — *lakum* — where ayah 12 had spoken to the Prophet ﷺ in the singular (*ilayka*, *ṣadruka*). The renderings in the source material reflect two ways of taking the sentence: "If then they answer you not" points at the challenged idolaters failing to reply, while "But if your helpers fail you" points at the allies the previous ayah had invited them to summon, since they were told to call whomsoever they could. Either way the outcome is the same silence, and the same conclusion follows from it.

**And then the pivot.** The proof does not end in an argument won. It ends in *lā ilāha illā huwa* — "there is no god besides Him" — and a question: "Will you then be Muslims?" Maʿārif renders the force of that closing question as: *would you now believe and obey, or would you prefer to remain heedless as before?* The evidence has done its work; what remains is the will. Which is exactly consistent with what Maʿārif said about the angel: Allah does not use material means to compel belief. He establishes the proof, and then He invites.

## Living it

**Do not trim the message to make it palatable.** The one thing they most wanted removed was the truth about their idols — and ayah 12 exists to make certain that not a word of it was removed. Anyone who carries this message will feel the same pull: to soften the part that offends the audience most. The answer is the same answer.

**A tight chest is not a failure of faith.** Allah named the constriction in His Messenger's ﷺ breast before He addressed it — and Ibn Kathir reads the whole statement as comfort. Grief at rejection is not a fault to be hidden; it is something Allah sees and speaks to directly.

**Deliver, then let go.** *But you are only a warner. And Allah is a Guardian over all things.* The duty is the calling; the outcome belongs to Allah. The consolation Ibn Kathir brings is worth keeping close — the Messengers before were rejected and harmed, yet they were patient until the help of Allah came to them.

**Warn the way a *nadhīr* warns** — out of love and affection for the one being warned, so that the warning itself carries glad tidings within it.

**And read the Qur'an knowing what it is.** The question at the end of ayah 14 is not aimed only at the Makkans of that day. The case has been made — will you then submit?

passages.title: Wanting only this world versus clear proof
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These three ayat weigh two lives against each other: the person whose entire aim is this world and its glitter (ayat 15–16), and the person who relies on a clear proof from his Lord (ayah 17). Ayah 17 opens with a question — in Ibn Kathir's rendering, *"Can they who rely on a clear proof from their Lord…"*, or as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān paraphrases it, *"Can a denier of the Qur'an be equal to the one who adheres to the Qur'an that has come from his Lord?"* Maʿārif puts the structure plainly: ayah 17 presents the high ground the Prophet ﷺ and the purely sincere believers with him occupy.

## The objection being answered

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the setting: when warnings of punishment were given to the opponents of Islam, they referred to the charities they contributed to and the social welfare work they did. With this testimonial of good deeds in their hands, why would they be punished? Maʿārif notes that in our time too there are Muslims who look at non-Muslims active in social work, giving in charity, making roads, bridges, hospitals, and are led to the opinion that they were better than Muslims. Ayah 15 is the answer.

That answer, in Maʿārif's summary: every deed, to be accepted as a source of salvation in the Hereafter, must fulfil the first condition of absolute sincerity — that it should have been done for the sake of Allah. And the only valid way of doing it for Allah is in accordance with the way taught and shown in practice by His Messenger ﷺ. A person who does not believe in Allah and His Messenger is one whose deeds and morals are, in Maʿārif's striking image, "a skeleton without soul": it may look handsome, but having no soul or spirit, it has no weight or effect in the home of the Hereafter.

And yet the deed is not thrown away entirely. Such a person's contribution really did benefit people, and in outward form what he did was good; so Allah, in consideration of His supreme equity and justice, has not allowed this deed to go to waste totally. Things are arranged instead in terms of the objectives the doers had: if they worked for recognition in society, an image as philanthropist or man of charity, or simply aspired for health, wealth and comfort, Allah lets them have all this right here in this world. Their deeds, being without the essential spirit, could not have qualified them to deserve salvation there. Therefore no return waits for them there, while the added burden of disbelief and disobedience remains.

## The wording of ayah 15: a settled habit, not a passing wish

Maʿārif draws attention to the expression. The Qur'an does not use something brief like **مَن أَرَادَ** *(man arāda)*, "those who wanted." It says **مَن كَانَ يُرِيدُ** *(man kāna yurīdu)*, "those who have been intending" — an expression that, as Maʿārif explains, denotes continuity and carries the sense of "kept striving for" — the settled orientation of a life.

Maʿārif spells this out: it is the condition of people who never wanted anything out of what they did but the good of this world, and never worried about the life to come. **As for the person who feels concerned about the Hereafter and does what would bring salvation there and, along with it, aims and plans to have his share from the world — he is not included in the purview of this verse at all.** Wanting *only* the world is what is condemned.

The verse then says such people are paid **in full** in this world, with **no diminution** — nothing, as Maʿārif puts it, is cut short in Dunya. Ibn Kathir preserves a measure of this from Ibn ʿAbbas, reported by al-ʿAwfi: those who show off "will be given their reward for their good deeds in this life. This will be so that they are not wronged, even the amount equivalent to the size of the speck on a date-stone." The payment is exact, and made in the currency they asked for.

Ayah 16 closes the account: nothing in the Hereafter but Fire — and, as Ibn Kathir renders it, "vain are the deeds they did therein. And of no effect is that which they used to do."

## Who exactly is this about? The scholars differ

Ibn Kathir gathers the early views. **Ibn ʿAbbas** applied it to showing off: whoever does a good deed — like fasting, prayer, or standing for prayer at night — in order to acquire worldly benefit, then Allah says, "Give him the reward of that which he sought in the worldly life," and his deed is wasted; in the Hereafter he will be of the losers. A similar narration has been reported from **Mujahid**, **Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk** and many others. **Anas bin Malik** and **Al-Ḥasan** both said the verse was revealed concerning the Jews and the Christians; **Mujahid** and others said it concerned the people who perform deeds to be seen. **Qatādah** said: whoever's concern, intention and goal is this worldly life, Allah will reward him for his good deeds in this life; then in the next life he will not have any good deeds to be rewarded — whereas the believer is rewarded in this life and in the Hereafter as well.

Maʿārif frames the disagreement: is this verse related to kafirs, to Muslims, or to both? Major authorities in Tafsir differ.

- **Disbelievers only.** The last sentence of the verse — that for them there is nothing in the Hereafter except the fire of Hell — seems to suggest this, because a Muslim, no matter how sinning, would ultimately go to Paradise after undergoing the punishment of sins. Therefore Ḍaḥḥāk and other commentators have interpreted it as related to kafirs only.
- **Muslims too.** Some commentators said it refers to Muslims who, through their good deeds, aim to acquire only the comfort, wealth and recognition of this worldly life; on that reading the closing sentence means that until they undergo the punishment of their evil deeds, they would have nothing except the fire of Hell.
- **The view Maʿārif calls weightier and clearer:** the verse relates to people who do their good deeds only with the intention of acquiring worldly benefits, such as wealth, health and recognition. They may be disbelievers who do not believe in the Hereafter from the very outset; or Muslims who believe in the Hereafter theoretically but do not apply their belief practically, keeping all concerns of their life attached to worldly benefits. From among the early commentators, Maʿārif reports, **Mujahid**, **Maimūn ibn Mihrān** and **Sayyidunā Muʿāwiyah** (may Allah be pleased with him) have gone by this view — the uncomfortable reading, since it does not let a believing reader file the verse under "them."

## From the Sunnah

Maʿārif notes that this meaning is supported by the well-known hadith of the Prophet ﷺ: **إِنَّمَا الأَعْمَالُ بِالنِّيَّاتِ** — *"Actions are [judged] according to intentions."* Whoever intends to have Dunya gets Dunya; whoever intends to have Akhirah gets Akhirah; whoever intends both gets both. That all actions depend on intention is, Maʿārif adds citing Qurtubi, a principle approved of in every community and religion.

Maʿārif then relates a hadith about those who devoted themselves to acts of worship in order to look respectable before others. On the Day of Qiyamah they will be brought forth and told: *you said your prayers, gave in charity, fought in Jihad, recited the Qur'an — but you did all that with the intention that you should be known as devotees to prayers, givers in charity, veteran warriors and great reciters. Now you have had what you wanted; the honours you were looking for have already come to you in the mortal world, and there is no return for your deeds here.* And these people, the hadith says, will be the first to be thrown into Hell. Maʿārif records that while reporting this hadith, **Sayyidunā Abū Hurairah** (may Allah be pleased with him) broke into tears and said that ayah 15 confirms it.

**Sahih Muslim**, on the authority of **Sayyidunā Anas** (may Allah be pleased with him), reports the Prophet ﷺ saying that Allah does no injustice to anyone: for the good deed a believer does, he gets some return in the mortal world while the real reward is in the Hereafter; as for a kafir, his account is cleared within his life here — the return for his good deeds is given in the form of worldly wealth, recognition, health and comfort, until he reaches the Hereafter with nothing left to bring any return.

**Jāmiʿ Tirmidhī** and the **Musnad of Ahmad**, again on the authority of **Sayyidunā Anas** (may Allah be pleased with him), report the Prophet ﷺ saying that whoever intends to have the best of the Hereafter, Allah makes his heart need-free in this world, Himself takes care of what he must have, and the world comes to him all humbled; and whoever intends to have the best of the present world, Allah makes want and need stand before him — no sooner does one need get fulfilled than another stands before him, and what he gets is only what Allah has written for him.

Maʿārif also cites Tafsir Mazhari: though a believer looks forward to prosperity in the mortal world too, his intention for the best of the Hereafter remains on top of everything; therefore he gets in this world only to the measure of his needs, while the larger reward is his in the Hereafter.

Also from Mazhari: **Sayyidunā ʿUmar** (may Allah be pleased with him) once visited the home of the Prophet ﷺ, and seeing virtually nothing in the house, said to him: please pray that Allah blesses your Ummah too with extended material means — we see Persia and Byzantium, very prosperous in this world although they do not worship Allah. The Prophet ﷺ had been reclining on a pillow; hearing this he sat up straight and said: *"O ʿUmar, you are still lost in those thoughts. As for these people, they are the ones who have been given the return of their good deeds right here in this world."*

## "But some chase the world and never get it"

Maʿārif raises a doubt: many people, despite striving to have worldly benefits, fail to achieve their objective even in this world, and on occasions get nothing.

The answer: the Qur'an deals with the subject briefly here, and details appear in Sūrah al-Isrāʾ — *"whoever keeps aspiring for the immediate, We shall give soon what We will to whom We will."* Two restrictions sit in that wording. Firstly, Allah gives **as much as He wants**, not necessarily what matches their desires. Secondly, He gives **only to a person it is appropriate to give according to His wisdom**; giving to everyone is not necessary. Ibn Kathir cites the same passage (17:18–21), where those who desire the Hereafter and strive for it while believers are "the ones whose striving shall be appreciated," and pairs it with 42:20: *"Whosoever desires the reward of the Hereafter, We give him increase in his reward, and whosoever desires the reward of this world, We give him thereof, and he has no portion in the Hereafter."*

## Ayah 17: the one who relies on a clear proof

**بَيِّنَة** *(bayyinah)* is the word rendered "clear proof." Maʿārif states that it refers to the Qur'an, and Ibn Kathir says this clear proof which is recited is the Qur'an, which Jibrīl conveyed to the Prophet ﷺ and which he ﷺ conveyed to his Ummah.

Ibn Kathir reads the ayah as Allah informing us of the believers' condition: they are upon **the natural religion of Allah (fiṭrah)** which He made inherent in His creatures — based upon their confession that there is none worthy of worship except He. He cites *"So set you your face towards the religion, Hanifan. Allah's Fitrah with which He has created mankind"* (30:30). **In the Two Sahihs** it is recorded that **Abu Hurayrah** said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Every child is born upon the Fitrah, but his parents make him a Jew, Christian, or Magian. This is just as the calf that is born whole. Have you noticed any calves that are born mutilated?"* And **in Sahih Muslim** it is recorded that **ʿIyad bin Himar** said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Allah, the Exalted, says, 'Verily, I created my servants Hunafa', but the devils came to them and distracted them from their religion. They made unlawful for them what I had made lawful for them and they commanded them to associate partners with Me, concerning which no authority has been revealed.'"* Ibn Kathir's conclusion: the believer is one who **remains** upon this fiṭrah.

**"And whom a witness from Him recites (follows) it"** — *wa yatlūhu shāhidun minhu*. Maʿārif notes that the authorities of tafsir differ over the meaning of *shāhid*.

- **Ibn Kathir**: a witness comes to him from Allah, and that witness is the pure, perfect and magnificent legislation that Allah revealed to the Prophets — legislations finalised with the Sharīʿah of Muhammad ﷺ. The believer's natural disposition bears witness to the truth of that legislation and accepts that specific laws are taken from it. In his phrase: **the fiṭrah accepts the Sharīʿah and believes in it.**
- **The author of Bayān al-Qurʼān**, as reported in Maʿārif, takes *shāhid* to mean **the miracle of the Qur'an that is present in the Qur'an as such** — so those who adhere to it already have, within it, a witness to its own veracity.

**"And before it, came the Book of Musa"** — Ibn Kathir: before the Qur'an there was the Book of Musa, the Tawrah, which Allah revealed to that Ummah **إِمَامًا وَرَحْمَةً**, as a leader and a guide for them to follow, and a mercy upon them. Whoever believed in it with true faith, it would lead him to believe in the Qur'an as well — hence *"they believe therein."* Maʿārif makes the same connection: the other witness has already come in the form of the Torah, which Sayyidunā Musa (peace be upon him) brought as guidance and mercy, and which confirms the truth of the Qur'an clearly.

## The warning, and the reassurance

**"But those of the sects that reject it, the Fire will be their promised meeting place."** Ibn Kathir reads *al-aḥzāb* — "the sects" — at full width: this is directed towards everyone who disbelieves in the Qur'an, whether they are idolators, disbelievers, People of the Scripture, or other sects from the descendants of Adam. He supports it with *"that I may therewith warn you and whomsoever it may reach"* (6:19) and *"Say: 'O mankind! Verily, I am sent to you all as the Messenger of Allah'"* (7:158). Maʿārif states the same point: anyone from any religion or community who refuses to have faith in the Prophet ﷺ will have his abode in Jahannam.

Both sources bring the Sunnah to bear:

- Ibn Kathir: **in Sahih Muslim** it is recorded that **Abu Musa Al-Ashʿari** (may Allah be pleased with him) said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"By He in Whose Hand is my soul! there is no one of this Ummah, whether he be a Jew or Christian, who hears of me and does not believe in me, except that he will enter the Hell-fire."*
- Maʿārif: **the Sahih of Muslim** reports on the authority of **Sayyidunā Abū Hurairah** (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet ﷺ said: *"by the One in whose hands rests my life, any Jew or Christian who hears my call and still does not believe in the teachings I have brought, then, he or she will be of the people of Jahannam."*

Ibn Kathir adds a note. **Saʿid bin Jubayr**, as reported from him by Ayyub as-Sakhtiyani, said that he never heard a hadith of the Prophet ﷺ, substantiated as he stated it, without finding its confirmation in the Qur'an. When this hadith reached Saʿid, he asked where its verification stood in the Book of Allah — and found it in this very phrase, which, he said, means from all religions.

Maʿārif draws the practical conclusion: this should remove the misunderstanding of those who regard the Jews and Christians, or adherents of other religions, as upon the truth on the basis of some outward deeds sufficient for salvation without faith in the Prophet ﷺ and the Qur'an. That position, it says, is in open clash with this ayah and with the authentic ahadith.

The ayah then turns to the Prophet ﷺ and to every reader after him: **"So be not in doubt about it. Verily, it is the truth from your Lord."** Ibn Kathir: the Qur'an is the truth from Allah and there is no doubt or suspicion concerning it — as in *"Alif Lam Mim. The revelations of the Book in which there is no doubt, is from the Lord of all that exists!"* (32:1–2).

And the last clause is a mercy for anyone who feels outnumbered: **"but most of mankind believe not."** Ibn Kathir gathers its companions across the Qur'an — *"And most of mankind will not believe even if you desire it eagerly"* (12:103) and *"And indeed Iblis did prove true his thought about them: and they followed him, all except a group of true believers"* (34:20). Numbers were never the measure of truth.

## Living it

What the passage asks is a check on **what a deed is for**. Ibn ʿAbbas' list is made of good things — fasting, prayer, standing for prayer at night — because the danger is precisely there: the act is sound and the aim has quietly slipped. And since ayah 15 says *kāna yurīdu* — continuity, in Maʿārif's reading — the question is not one moment of vanity but the drift of a life: what have I been intending?

Ayah 17 offers the alternative: a person relying on a clear proof from his Lord, with revelation confirming what his created nature already knew — and, in the hadith of Jāmiʿ Tirmidhī and the Musnad of Ahmad, a heart Allah makes need-free while the world comes to him all humbled.

passages.title: Fabricators exposed and the two parties compared
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is.** These seven ayat put two kinds of people side by side and follow each to the end of the road. Ayat 18–22 take the person who invents lies about Allah, bring him into open court on the Day of Judgement, and total up what his lie finally cost him. Ayat 23–24 answer with the believers — and then close by asking the reader a question he cannot dodge: are these two alike?

What holds the unit together is a single courtroom logic. It opens with a question (*who does more wrong…*), summons witnesses, pronounces a curse, seals off every escape route, delivers the verdict, names the loss — and then stands both parties together for comparison.

## Ayah 18: dragged into open court

The ayah begins with a comparative: **wa man aẓlamu** — "and who does *more* wrong?" It is a question that expects no answer, because there is none. Of all the wrongs a human being can commit, inventing a lie **against Allah** (*iftarā ʿalā Allāhi kadhiban*) is placed at the top.

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is here describing the condition of those who lie against Him, and that **their scandal in the Hereafter will be presented before the heads of creation** — the angels, the Messengers, the Prophets, and the rest of mankind and the jinn. That is the force of "such will be brought before their Lord, and the witnesses will say, *These are the ones who lied against their Lord!*" The lie was told in public; the exposure is public too.

**From the Sunnah — the two ways of being questioned.** Ibn Kathir brings a narration here that transforms the ayah. Imam Ahmad recorded from Safwan bin Muhriz, who said: "I was holding the hand of Ibn ʿUmar when a man was brought to him.
