The man asked, 'How did you hear the Messenger of Allah ﷺ describe *An-Najwa* — secret counsel or confidential talk — on the Day of Resurrection?' Ibn ʿUmar said, 'I heard him say:

> Verily, Allah, the Mighty and Sublime, will draw near the believer and He will place His shade over him. He will conceal him from the people and make him confess to his sins. He will say to him, "Do you recognise this sin? Do you recognise that sin? Do you recognise such and such sin?" This will continue until He makes him confess to all of his sins and he will think to himself that he is about to be destroyed. Then Allah will say, "Verily, I have concealed these sins for you in the worldly life and I have forgiven you for them today." Then he will be given his Book of good deeds. As for the disbelievers and the hypocrites, the witnesses will say: **These are the ones who lied against their Lord! No doubt! The curse of Allah is on the wrongdoers.**'"

Ibn Kathir notes that **both Al-Bukhari and Muslim recorded this narration in the Two Sahihs.**

Notice what the hadith does. The believer's reckoning is a *private* conversation — drawn near, screened from the people, walked through his own record until he is certain he is finished, and then forgiven. The wrongdoer's reckoning is the exact opposite: not a whisper but an announcement, in front of everyone. The same Day holds both a covering and an unveiling.

The ayah ends with the announcement itself: *No doubt! The curse of Allah is on the wrongdoers.* The word "wrongdoers" (*ẓālimīn*) closes the circle opened by "who does more **wrong**" at the start.

## Ayah 19: the three-part description

Ayah 19 does not describe passive unbelievers. It describes an active programme, in three moves:

**1. "They hinder others from the path of Allah."** Ibn Kathir: this means they prevent people from following the truth and from travelling upon the path of guidance that leads to Allah. And in doing so, he adds, **they also keep the people away from Paradise itself.** The obstruction is not academic; it has an eternal cost, and not only their own.

**2. "And seek a crookedness therein" (*yabghūnahā ʿiwajan*).** Ibn Kathir: they want their path to be **crooked and uneven**. This is subtler than blocking the road — it is bending it. Not "there is no path," but "the path runs *this* way," until what is straight is presented as bent and what is bent is presented as straight.

**3. "While they are disbelievers in the Hereafter."** Ibn Kathir: they deny the Hereafter, rejecting the idea that any of its events will occur or that any of it exists at all. This is the engine underneath the other two. A man who genuinely expects to stand before Allah does not casually invent claims about Him. Remove the Last Day and the lie costs nothing.

## Ayah 20: no escape, no protector, and the doubled punishment

**"They will never frustrate Allah on earth"** — in Ibn Kathir's rendering, "by no means will they escape on earth." His gloss is stark: these disbelievers are **under the power of Allah and His force; they are in His grasp and are subject to His authority**, and He is Most Able to exact vengeance against them in this life before the coming of the Hereafter. "Nor have they protectors besides Allah" removes the second exit: no protector besides Him.

**Then why do they seem to get away with it?** Ibn Kathir anticipates the objection and answers it with the Qur'an's own words — *but He gives them respite up to a Day when the eyes will stare in horror* (14:42) — and with a hadith recorded **in the Two Sahihs**, that the Prophet ﷺ said:

> Verily Allah gives respite to the oppressor until He seizes him, then he will not be able to escape Him.

Delay is not indifference. It is rope.

**"Their torment will be doubled."** Ibn Kathir gives the reason, and it is worth sitting with: the torment is doubled **because Allah gave them hearing, vision and hearts, but these things did not benefit them.** Rather, they were deaf from hearing the truth and blinded away from following it. He cites their own words from the Fire — *Had we but listened or used our intelligence, we would not have been among the dwellers of the blazing Fire* (67:10) — and the verse *Those who disbelieved and hindered others from the path of Allah, for them We will add torment to the torment* (16:88). For this reason, he says, they will be punished **for every command that they abandoned and every prohibition that they indulged in.**

The faculties named here — hearing and sight — are precisely the faculties that will return in ayah 24 as the whole point of the parable.

## Ayat 21–22: what the loss actually was

**"It is they who have ruined themselves" (*khasirū anfusahum*).** Of everything a person can lose, they lost the one thing that could not be replaced: themselves. Ibn Kathir explains this concretely — they will be made to enter a blazing Fire where they are punished, and its torment will not be lifted from them **for even the blinking of an eye**; as Allah says, *Whenever it abates, We shall increase for them the fierceness of the Fire* (17:97).

**"And whatever they invented eluded them" (*ḍalla ʿanhum*).** Ibn Kathir's gloss on *ḍalla ʿanhum* is simply: **it has left them.** What "they invented" refers to what they set up besides Allah — rivals and idols — and, Ibn Kathir stresses, these things **did not avail them in the slightest; in fact they actually caused them great harm.** He supports this with *And when mankind are gathered, they will become their enemies and will deny their worshipping* (46:6), and *When those who were followed disown those who followed them, and they see the torment, then all their relations will be cut off from them* (2:166).

This is the sting of the passage. The fabrication does not merely fail to help — everything the man built his life on walks away at the moment he needs it, and then joins the case against him.

**"Without a doubt, they will be the worst losers in the Hereafter" (ayah 22).** The verdict comes with *lā jarama* — "no doubt about it" — and with a superlative: *al-akhsarūn*, not merely losers but **the greatest losers**. Ibn Kathir reads the whole thing as a transaction gone catastrophically wrong. In their trade for the abode of the Hereafter they:

- exchanged the highest levels of Paradise for the lowest levels of Hell;
- substituted the pleasure of Gardens for the fierce boiling water of Hell;
- exchanged the drink of sealed nectar for the fierce hot wind, boiling water and a shade of black smoke;
- chose food from the filth of dirty wounds instead of wide-eyed lovely maidens;
- preferred *Hawiyah* — a pit in Hell — instead of lofty castles;
- and chose the anger of Allah and His punishment over nearness to Him and the blessing of gazing at Him.

"Therefore," Ibn Kathir concludes, "it is no injustice that such people should be the greatest losers in the Hereafter." They were not robbed. They traded, and this is what they accepted in return.

## Ayah 23: the other party

Having mentioned the condition of the wretched, Ibn Kathir says, Allah now **commends the people of delight** — the believers — and describes them in three parts that map onto a whole human being:

- **"Those who believe"** — their *hearts* believed.
- **"and do good"** — their *limbs* worked righteous deeds, both in statements and actions; this includes their performance of deeds of obedience and their abandonment of evils. Faith that stayed in the chest and never reached the hands is not what is being described.
- **"and humble themselves before their Lord"** (*akhbatū ilā rabbihim*) — the inner posture underneath both. Read against ayat 18–22, this is the exact reverse of the fabricator: he spoke about Allah what Allah never said; these people lower themselves *before* Allah.

Their reward, in Ibn Kathir's description: they are the inheritors of Gardens containing lofty rooms and seats arranged in rows, bunches of fruit near to them, elevated couches, fair and beautiful wives, various types of fruit, desired kinds of food and delicious drinks. **They will also be allowed to see the Creator of the heavens and the earth** — what Ibn Kathir called above "the blessing of gazing at Him," the very thing the losing party traded away.

And it does not end. They will be in this state of pleasure forever: they will not die, nor will they grow old; they will not experience sickness, nor will they sleep; there will be no excrement, no spit, no snot — **their sweat will be the perfume of musk.**

## Ayah 24: the parable that closes the argument

*The example of these two parties is that of the blind and the deaf, and the seeing and the hearing.*

Ibn Kathir explains that "the two parties" (*al-farīqayn*) refers back to exactly the two groups just described: those disbelievers whom Allah first described as wretched, and then those believers whom He described with delightfulness. The first group is like one who is blind and deaf; the second like he who sees and hears.

**The disbeliever** is blind from the truth in this life and in the Hereafter — not guided to goodness, and not even recognising it. He is deaf from hearing the proofs, so he does not hear that which would benefit him. Ibn Kathir cites: *Had Allah known of any good in them, He would indeed have made them listen* (8:23).

**The believer**, in Ibn Kathir's striking phrase, is **"smart, bright and clever."** He sees the truth and distinguishes between the truth and falsehood, so he follows the good and abandons the evil. He hears, and he distinguishes between the proof and scepticism — and therefore **falsehood does not overcome him.** Faith is portrayed here not as blind acceptance but as functioning eyesight and working hearing: the capacity to tell the difference. "Are these two types of people alike?"

Now look back. Ayah 20 said their punishment is doubled because *"they could not bear to listen and they used not to see."* Ayah 24 turns that into their permanent description: blind and deaf. The faculties they refused to use became the name they carry.

**"Will you not then take heed?"** (*afalā tadhakkarūn*). Ibn Kathir reads this as: *will you not consider, so that you may distinguish between these two categories of people?* The comparison is not offered for the losing party's benefit; it is put to **you**, the listener, to make you sort yourself. He brings the parallels: *Not equal are the dwellers of the Fire and the dwellers of Paradise; it is the dwellers of Paradise that will be successful* (59:20), and the sequence *Not alike are the blind and the seeing; nor darkness and light; nor the shade and the sun's heat; nor the living and the dead…* (35:19–24).

And note that the word is a dual — *al-farīqayn*, two parties. The passage offers no third category to stand in.

## Living it

- **Guard your speech about Allah.** Ayah 18 does not begin with the worst *deed*; it begins with the worst *claim* — something said about Allah that He never said. "Allah has forbidden," "Allah has permitted," "Allah wants" — said without knowledge, this is the ground of ayah 18. Where you do not know, say you do not know.
- **Weigh your influence, not only your own record.** Ayah 19 describes people whose damage did not stop at themselves; Ibn Kathir says they also keep the people away from Paradise itself. Anyone whose words shape how others see the religion — a parent, a teacher, someone with an audience — should feel that weight.
- **Do not misread a quiet life as approval.** Ayah 20 with the hadith of the Two Sahihs settles it: the rope given to the wrongdoer is not a pardon.
- **Use the two faculties you were given.** The doubling in ayah 20 was tied to hearing and sight that went unused. The remedy is exactly what ayah 24 praises: actually listen to the proof, actually look at the truth, and train yourself to distinguish it from what merely sounds like it.
- **Check all three parts of ayah 23.** Belief in the heart, deeds in the limbs, and humility before Allah underneath both. It is possible to have two of the three and be missing the one that holds them up.
- **Answer the closing question honestly.** *Will you not then take heed?* Ibn Kathir says it means: consider, and distinguish. The passage is not finished until the reader has placed himself in one of the two parties.

passages.title: Noah's call, the chiefs' contempt, and his answer
passages.tafsir:
Seven ayat, one scene. Nūḥ (peace be upon him) opens his mission with two short sentences, the ruling class of his people answers with a sneer, and the rest of the passage is his reply. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that when Nūḥ invited his people to believe, they responded with doubts and objections against the truth of his mission as a prophet and messenger of Allah — and that, by Allah's will and permission, he answered them. Three charges are laid in ayah 27, and ayat 28–31 are a patient defence that never once accepts the accusers' terms.

## The first Messenger, and the smallest possible message

Ibn Kathir tells us who this man was: Nūḥ was **the first Messenger whom Allah sent to the people of the earth**, a people who were polytheists involved in the worship of idols.

His opening statement in ayah 25 is one phrase: *innī lakum nadhīrun mubīn* — "I am to you a plain warner." Ibn Kathir explains **nadhīr mubīn** as warning you *openly* against facing Allah's punishment if you persist in worshipping other than Allah.

Ayah 26 gives the content: *an lā taʿbudū illā-llāh* — "that you worship none but Allah" — followed immediately by "surely I fear for you the punishment of a painful Day," which Ibn Kathir reads as: if you continue in this, Allah will punish you with a severe punishment in the Hereafter. The command is pure tawḥīd; the motive is not contempt but **fear on their behalf**: he does not say "I fear you" but "I fear *for* you."

## The chiefs' three charges (ayah 27)

The reply comes from *al-malaʾ alladhīna kafarū* — the disbelieving chiefs. Ibn Kathir defines **al-malaʾ** as the leaders and the heads of the disbelievers. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds: *malaʾ* generally means a group, and leading lexicographers say that a group made up of the *chiefs* of a people is called *malaʾ*.

**One: "You are only a human being like us."** Ibn Kathir renders their thinking: *you are not an angel; you are only a human, so how can revelation come to you over us?* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān spells it out: he eats, drinks, walks, sleeps and wakes exactly as we do. They held that a messenger sent to men should not belong to the genus of man at all, but should be an angel, whose distinct rank everyone would be forced to acknowledge, willing or unwilling.

**Two: "Only the lowest of us follow you, and they did it without thinking."** *Arādhil* is the plural of *ardhal*, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān defines as someone lowly, having no status or respect among his people. Ibn Kathir: the followers are the likes of merchants and weavers — no nobility, no rulers among them. The phrase *bādiya al-raʾy* means, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's words, **a cursory or shallow opinion**; Ibn Kathir explains it as following the first thing that came into their minds.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out two layers here. The first is an argument: *if your call were true, the people of higher status would have accepted it first.* The second is no argument at all but a condition of the ego: *suppose we did believe — then we would be counted Muslims like them and equal to them, and in the rows of prayer and in other gatherings we would have to sit with them as equals. This we cannot do.* That is the real obstacle.

**Three: "We see no merit in you over us — in fact we think you are liars."** Ibn Kathir unpacks it: *we do not see that you and your followers have gained any virtuous status above us in your physical appearance, your character, your provisions or your condition, since you accepted this religion of yours.* And *naẓunnukum kādhibīn* — we think you are lying about what you claim for yourselves of righteousness, piety, worship, and happiness in the abode of the Hereafter when you arrive there.

## Why the objection collapses

Ibn Kathir calls this response a proof of the chiefs' ignorance and their deficiency in knowledge and intelligence, and answers the second charge with a principle: **the truth is not to be rejected because of the lowly status of those who follow it.** In fact, he says, the followers of the truth are the noble ones even if they are poor, while those who reject the truth are the lowly wretches even if they are wealthy — and in the Hereafter it is the rejecters who will be the greatest losers.

He then notes the pattern: usually it is the weakest of people who follow the truth, while the nobility and the high-class people oppose it — as Allah says of every town to which a warner was sent, that it was **the luxurious ones** (*mutrafūhā*) who answered, "We found our fathers following a certain way and religion, and we will indeed follow their footsteps" (43:23). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the reason: honour and disgrace, reason and understanding are not subservient to wealth and property. Power and wealth can become intoxicating enough to stop their possessors from understanding and accepting things that are perfectly reasonable and correct. Those barriers do not stand before the meek and the poor. This has been the customary Divine practice down the ages, and it was explained in past Scriptures too.

Both commentaries relate the same incident. Ibn Kathir: when Heraclius, the emperor of Rome, asked Abū Sufyān Ṣakhr ibn Ḥarb about the qualities of the Prophet ﷺ, he said to him, "Are his followers the noble people, or the weak?" Abū Sufyān said, "They are the weakest of them." Heraclius replied, "They are the followers of the Messengers." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the setting: the Prophet's ﷺ letter of invitation had reached the Byzantine emperor, who had read the signs of the noble prophets in the Torah and the Injīl and assembled people of Arabia then visiting Syria to ask them about those signs; on hearing the answer he confessed that this itself was a sign of his being a true prophet, since those who follow prophets initially are these very poor and weak people. The chiefs of Nūḥ's people offered as proof of falsehood the very thing a well-read outsider recognised as proof of truth.

**And the insult *bādiya al-raʾy* turns out to be no insult at all.** Ibn Kathir says it is not objectionable or derogatory, because the truth, once made clear, does not leave room for second-guessing or excessive thinking. Rather, it is *mandatory* that it be followed, and this is the condition of every pious, intelligent person. No one continues doubtfully pondering the truth after it has been made clear except one who is ignorant and excessively critical — and the Messengers, Allah's peace and blessings be upon them all, only ever delivered what was obvious and clear. As for "we see no merit in you," Ibn Kathir says they did not see it because they were blind from the truth: they could neither see nor hear, but were wavering in their skepticism, wandering blindly in the darknesses of their ignorance.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān redefines the word they had thrown around. In reality *radhīl* — disgraced — is the one who does not recognise his Creator and Sustainer and disobeys what He has asked him to do. It records how early scholars answered when asked who is mean and disgraced: Sufyān ibn Saʿīd ath-Thawrī said, "people who keep flattering rulers and officials." Ibn al-ʿArabī said, "mean is he who earns dunyā by selling his dīn," and, asked who is the meanest, "a person who ruins his religion and streamlines the worldly life of someone else." Imām Mālik said, "mean is he who maligns the noble Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, because they are the greatest benefactors of the entire Muslim Ummah, and the source through which the blessings of īmān and the Sharīʿah have reached us."

## Nūḥ's answer: a clear proof, and no compulsion (ayah 28)

He begins *yā qawmi* — "O my people." He is still claiming them, even now.

Then: "Tell me — if I am upon a **bayyinah** from my Lord, and a mercy has come to me from Him, but it has been obscured from your sight, shall we compel you to accept it while you have a strong hatred for it?" Ibn Kathir explains **bayyinah** as certainty, a clear matter, and truthful prophethood — and that this is the greatest mercy from Allah upon Nūḥ *and upon them*. *Fa-ʿummiyat ʿalaykum* means it was hidden from you and you were not guided to it, so you did not know its importance and hastily rejected and denied it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān treats this ayah as the reply to the first charge: **for a messenger to be a man is not contrary to his mission; a little thought shows this is how it should be.** The messenger of men should be a man, so that men find it comfortable to learn their religion from him. An angel is not hungry or thirsty or sleepy or plain tired, and carries none of the human compulsions — how would he have the feeling for such human weaknesses, and without that feeling how could men have followed him deed-wise? What a messenger genuinely needs is not a different species but **proof, argument and evidence from Allah** that he was truly sent, and for ordinary people those open proofs take the form of the miracles shown at the hands of prophets. Had they looked at it carefully and thought about it, they would not have refused; their aversion and hostility made them blind, so they opted to deny the truth and became adamant in it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: this mercy of Allah that comes through a prophet is not something that can be caused to fall over the heads of people until they themselves show an inclination to have it. There is a hint here that the prophet would have passed on the wealth of īmān he had come with, despite all their denial and obstinacy, if only he could — but that was against Divine law. **A blessing is aspired for; people cannot be compelled to have it.** From this it also stands proved that in no prophet's era was it ever permissible to compel people to become believers. Those who keep spreading the propaganda that Islam was spread by the sword are not themselves unaware of the truth of the matter; they find it convenient to use the power of a lie to sow seeds of doubt in the hearts of the ignorant.

This, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, also explains why an angel was not made a prophet. An angel is endowed with supernatural power and is way distinct from human beings in every facet of his existence; to *see* him and then believe in him would have become an exercise in compulsion — with an angel in front of him, who could dare being obstinate, as people so conveniently were before prophets? And according to the dictate of the Sharīʿah, if a person believes unwillingly under the threat of some coercive power, his belief is not acceptable. The ideally desirable thing is **al-īmān bi'l-ghayb** — to believe without having fully observed and witnessed the ultimate subduing power of Allah.

## "I will not drive away those who have believed" (ayat 29–30)

First, money: "I ask of you no wealth for it; my reward is from none but Allah." Ibn Kathir: *māl* here means payment that he takes from them; Nūḥ is only seeking the reward from Allah, the Mighty and Sublime. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the consequence: a prophet does not fancy anyone's wealth or property and takes no compensation for his counsel, so **the rich and the poor are equal in his sight** — let the rich not be scared about their wealth, for no one would start asking for it once they become believers.

Second, and harder: *wa mā anā bi-ṭāridi-lladhīna āmanū* — "I am not going to drive away those who have believed." Ibn Kathir: the disbelievers had actually *asked* Nūḥ to disassociate himself from the believers, because they were averse to them and felt themselves too important to sit with them. This is similar to the request made to the seal of the Messengers ﷺ, that he disassociate himself from a group of people considered weak in their social status and sit with the elite in a special gathering of their own — upon which, Ibn Kathir says, Allah revealed, "And turn not away those who invoke their Lord, morning and afternoon," and, "Thus We have tried some of them with others, that they might say, 'Is it these whom Allah has favoured from among us?' Does not Allah know best those who are grateful?" (6:53). It is the same demand, made to the first Messenger and to the last.

Nūḥ's refusal has two supports. The first is the honour of the scorned: Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders his answer as *they may be poor, but they are close to the Highest of the high — the greatest honour one can have; turning such people out is not a right thing to do.* The second is *innahum mulāqū rabbihim*, "they are surely to meet their Lord," which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes could also mean: if, supposedly, I were to turn them out, then when they go to their Lord on the Day of Qiyāmah and complain, what would I have to say?

Ayah 30 presses this into a question: **"Who will help me against Allah if I drove them away? Will you not then give a thought?"** And the verdict of ayah 29 — "I see that you are a people who are ignorant" — is, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, ignorance pulling in two opposite directions at once: to you, being a man is counter to being a prophet, and then you go to the other extreme and demand that poor people be driven from his company.

## What Nūḥ does not claim (ayah 31)

The passage ends with Nūḥ announcing matters of principle — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's summary is that the mission of a prophet and messenger does not depend on the things they imagine are necessary for it. Ibn Kathir frames it: Nūḥ is informing them that he is a Messenger from Allah, calling to the worship of Allah alone without any partners, and doing so by Allah's permission; he asks no reward for the work, and he invites whomever he meets, whether of nobility or low class — and whoever responds favourably has achieved salvation.

**"I do not say to you that with me are the treasures of Allah."** Ibn Kathir: he has no power to manipulate the hidden treasures of Allah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it as refuting their idea that someone coming from Allah as His messenger should arrive with treasures and hand them out freely — the mission of prophets has nothing to do with involving people in the mess of worldly enjoyments. It is also possible, it notes, that the statement refutes a false thought nursed by some people, that Allah has given all powers to prophets and even to the Awliyāʾ, so that they hold the treasures of Allah's power in their hands and decide who receives and who does not. Allah has not entrusted total control of the treasures of His power to any prophet, let alone to the Awliyāʾ. What is true is that when they pray or wish, **Allah** answers their prayers and fulfils their wishes with His infinite power.

**"Nor do I know the ghayb."** Ibn Kathir: he has no knowledge of the Unseen **except what Allah has allowed him to know**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the creed precisely: the mission of a prophet needs no knowledge of the unseen, and why should it, when knowledge of the unseen is an exclusive attribute of Allah which no prophet and no angel shares with Him. Allah does inform whichever of His prophets He wills about the secrets of the unseen, as much as He wills — but even so it is not correct to call them *ʿālim al-ghayb*, because it is not in their power to find out something in the domain of the unseen at their own choice.

**"Nor do I say that I am an angel."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: the refutation of their idea that a messenger should be an angel. He concedes their observation and — as ayah 28 has already shown — denies that it was ever a defect. He is, in Ibn Kathir's words, merely a human Messenger aided with miracles.

**And the fourth statement, which is about them, not him:** "nor do I say of those whom your eyes look down upon that Allah will not bestow any good on them — Allah knows what is in their inner selves." Ibn Kathir: if they are believers in their hearts as their condition appears to be outwardly, then they will have a good reward; and if anyone behaves evilly with them after they have believed, then he is a wrongdoer who speaks what he has no knowledge of. Nūḥ will not pronounce on hearts, because Allah knows best what is in their souls. **He refuses to despise the people they despise, and refuses as a matter of knowledge, not politeness** — the closing words are *innī idhan la-mina-ẓ-ẓālimīn*: "in that case I should indeed be one of the wrongdoers."

## Living it

- **Measure a call by its proof, not by its crowd.** Ibn Kathir's rule cuts both ways: do not reject truth because unimpressive people hold it, and do not accept falsehood because impressive people do.
- **Do not let truth wait on your pride.** If what stops you accepting something is that it would put you level with people you consider beneath you, that is the objection of the *malaʾ*, dressed up.
- **When truth is clear, act on it.** Prolonged doubt after clarity is the mark of the ignorant and the excessively critical, not the careful.
- **Never force faith, and never be discouraged that you cannot.** A blessing is aspired for; the caller's job is to make it clear, not compulsory.
- **Guard the standing of the poor believer.** The chiefs made their own belief conditional on the poor being expelled; Nūḥ answered that he simply could not do it.
- **Claim no more than Allah has given you.** No treasuries, no unseen, no angelic rank, and no verdicts on what is inside other people.

passages.title: They demand the punishment; Noah's final warning
passages.tafsir:
## The moment the argument ends

Nūḥ (Noah), peace be upon him, has been calling his people, and by their own account he has argued with them at length. Here they close the door. They do not answer his evidence; they announce that they have heard enough, and dare him to produce the punishment he has been warning them about (ayah 32). Ayat 33 and 34 are his reply — Ibn Kathir's heading for the section is *The People's Request of Nuh to bring the Torment and His Response to Them* — and ayah 35 steps out of the story altogether to address the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and the pagans of Makkah. What holds these ayat together is a single theme: **the caller delivers, and Allah alone decides.** Nūḥ does not own the punishment, does not own its timing, and does not decide the outcome in anyone's heart.

## "You have argued with us far too much"

Look closely at how they phrase their refusal in ayah 32: *qad jādaltanā fa-aktharta jidālanā* — "you have disputed with us, and much have you prolonged the dispute with us." The sentence names the act and then piles on its sheer quantity: first the disputing, then how much of it there has been. Ibn Kathir puts their meaning bluntly: they were saying, **"You have argued with us long enough, and we are still not going to follow you."**

That is a confession disguised as a complaint. Their grievance is that he argued too *much*, not that he argued badly. They produce no counter-argument in these words at all — only impatience, and a settled refusal that they state openly.

Then comes the dare: *fa'tinā bimā ta'idunā in kunta mina-ṣ-ṣādiqīn* — "now bring upon us what you threaten us with, if you are of the truthful." Ibn Kathir explains that what Nūḥ had "promised" them refers to the vengeance and torment from Allah, and that their words amount to saying: **"Supplicate against us however you wish, and let whatever you have supplicated come to us."** They were not asking a question. They were treating the warning as an empty threat and calling for it to be tested. Ibn Kathir opens the whole scene this way: Allah informs us that the people of Nūḥ **sought to hasten Allah's vengeance, torment, anger and the trial** — that is, His punishment — upon themselves. There are few more frightening things a person can ask for.

## Ayah 33: "It is Allah Who can bring it upon you if He wills"

Nūḥ does not rise to the dare. His answer is one of the great short lessons in the Qur'an on where power actually sits: *innamā ya'tīkum bihi-llāhu in shā'a wa mā antum bi-muʿjizīn.*

**"Only Allah will bring it."** They had told him to supplicate against them and let whatever he asked for arrive. He does not say "I will bring it," and he does not say "I will pray and it will come." Ibn Kathir spells out the force of his reply: **"It is only Allah Who can punish you and hasten your punishment for you."** The dare was aimed at Nūḥ; he steps out of the way and lets it land where it belongs.

**"In shā'a" — "if He wills."** Even having stripped himself of any claim on the punishment, Nūḥ does not then guarantee it on Allah's behalf. Its coming, and its timing, are tied to the divine will and to nothing else — not to their impatience, and not to his own wish.

**"Wa mā antum bi-muʿjizīn" — "and then you will escape not."** Ibn Kathir gives the point in a single line: **He is the One from Whom nothing escapes.** Their demand had assumed the matter was in Nūḥ's hands, as though the worst they faced was a man's supplication. His reply places it in Allah's hands and closes the other door too: there is no getting out of reach.

## Ayah 34: "My advice will not benefit you…"

The second half of his reply turns from Allah's power to the limits of Nūḥ's own role: *wa lā yanfaʿukum nuṣḥī in aradtu an anṣaḥa lakum in kāna-llāhu yurīdu an yughwiyakum* — "And my advice will not profit you, even if I wish to give you good counsel, if Allah's will is to keep you astray."

Ibn Kathir explains what "profit" would have meant here: **something that could be useful to you in accepting his preaching to them, his warning to them and his advising them.** That is the whole of a prophet's work in one phrase — preaching, warning, advising. And Nūḥ says, with startling honesty, that all of it cannot by itself produce acceptance in a heart.

On *an yughwiyakum*, Ibn Kathir's gloss is: **"your deception and your ultimate destruction."** Note carefully that Nūḥ frames it as a **condition** — "*if* Allah's will is…" — not as a verdict he is pronouncing on them. He is not telling them they are finished; he is telling them where the outcome is decided. Allah's will is real and effective, and the benefit of counsel rests on it. That does not lift the weight off them: ayah 32 has just recorded their refusal in their own words, and the ayah ends by reminding them where they are headed.

Then the closing line, which reframes everything: *huwa rabbukum wa ilayhi turjaʿūn* — **"He is your Lord, and to Him you shall return."** They had been speaking as though the punishment were an item on Nūḥ's agenda that he might or might not deliver. He answers that the One they are daring is **their own Lord** — not a rival power, not his private deity. Ibn Kathir unfolds this ending at length, and it is worth reading slowly. Allah is:

- **the Owner of the finality of all matters** — the last word in every affair is His;
- **the Controller, the Judge, the Most Just, who does not do any injustice** — so no one is wronged in what befalls them;
- **the One to whom belong the creation and the command** — both bringing things into being and directing them;
- **the Originator and the Repeater** of the creation — He begins it and brings it back again;
- **the Owner of this life and the Hereafter.**

Ibn Kathir here is listing what Allah has made known about Himself, and we affirm these as they came — without likening Him to His creation and without draining the words of their meaning. Their force in this context is plain: the very people daring Him to strike are living inside His dominion, on their way back to Him.

## Ayah 35: the story stops, and the Prophet ﷺ is addressed

*Am yaqūlūna-ftarāhu?* — "Or do they say: he has fabricated it?"

Ibn Kathir heads this ayah **"An Interruption to verify the Truthfulness of the Prophet ﷺ,"** and explains its purpose in one sentence: **"This is presented in the middle of the story to affirm the story itself."** The "they" here are the pagans of Makkah. It is as if Allah, the Exalted, is saying to Muhammad ﷺ: *or do these obstinate disbelievers say that he fabricated this and invented it himself?*

The reply he is told to give is remarkable for what it does *not* do. He does not swear an oath or demand belief. He says: *in iftaraytuhu fa-ʿalayya ijrāmī wa anā barī'un mimmā tujrimūn* — "if I have fabricated it, upon me be my crimes, but I am innocent of all those crimes which you commit." Ibn Kathir explains the first half simply: **such sin would be mine alone.** Nobody else carries it; the risk is entirely his own. And of the second half he says: **this story is not invented, or fabricated falsely — because he ﷺ knows better the punishment of Allah for one who lies about Allah.**

That last line is the real argument, and it is an argument from knowledge. The man they were accusing is the one who knows best what Allah does to someone who invents speech and attributes it to Him. Of all people, he is the least likely to take that gamble. Meanwhile the crimes they commit remain theirs, and he declares himself clear of them. It is the same shape of truth that runs through Nūḥ's reply: each person carries his own load, and the return is to Allah.

## Living it

**Deliver, then let go.** Nūḥ's entire reply in ayat 33–34 is a man refusing to claim what is not his — not the punishment, not its timing, not the acceptance of his counsel. If someone you love will not listen, you have not failed. You have done what Nūḥ did.

**Never call for punishment to be hastened.** Nūḥ's people told him to supplicate against them however he wished and let it come. Ibn Kathir describes them as **seeking to hasten Allah's vengeance, torment, anger and the trial** upon themselves. That is the mood of ayah 32 — impatience with a warning, turned into a request for the thing being warned about.

**Keep your counsel sincere even when it is refused.** Ayah 34 says plainly that acceptance was never in Nūḥ's hands, and he still wished to give them good counsel. The value of advice is not measured by the response it gets.

**Do not think anyone slips out of reach.** "You will escape not." Ibn Kathir: **He is the One from Whom nothing escapes.** That is a warning to the defiant and a comfort to the wronged — nothing and no one is outside Allah's reach.

**And remember the ending of ayah 34 when you feel small.** "He is your Lord, and to Him you shall return." The Owner of the finality of all matters, who begins the creation and brings it back, who judges and does no injustice — He is the One holding the matter you are worried about.

passages.title: Building the Ark under mocking eyes
passages.tafsir:
**In one breath:** after centuries of preaching that won only a handful of believers, Nuh (peace be upon him) is told that the door has closed — no one else from his people will ever believe. He is then handed a task that must have looked like madness: build a ship, on dry land, in full view of the men who despise him. Ayat 36–39 hang together as the hinge of his whole mission: the calling ends, the building begins, and the chiefs who stand around laughing are told precisely when the laughter will stop.

## What had already happened

To feel these four ayat you have to feel the exhaustion behind them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes the life this revelation interrupted. Allah gave Nuh (peace be upon him) an extraordinarily long life — extending up to nearly a thousand years — and gave those years a single purpose: to call people to Allah as One. He met the harshest of pains in that mission. His people would throw stones at him until he fell and lost consciousness; as soon as he came round, he would pray to Allah to forgive them, because they did not know what they were doing. One generation was followed by another, and that one by yet another, and he kept giving his call in the hope that at some stage they might accept the truth.

When centuries had passed over this exercise in patience, he laid his complaint before his Lord — the words preserved in Sūrah Nūḥ: "My Lord, I did invite my people night and day. But my invitation increased them in nothing but flight" (71:5–6) — and, after all those long years of hardship, the prayer of this great servant of Allah: "My Lord, help me because they have belied me" (al-Muʾminūn 23:26, 39).

Ibn Kathir sets the scene slightly differently. He says Allah sent this revelation when Nuh's people had *hastened* Allah's vengeance and punishment upon themselves, and Nuh then supplicated against them: "My Lord! Leave not one of the disbelievers inhabiting the earth" (71:26), and "I have been overcome, so help me!" (54:10). It was at that point, Ibn Kathir says, that Allah revealed the words of ayah 36.

Either way, this passage is an answer. A man who had spent a lifetime of centuries knocking on one door is finally told what is behind it.

## Ayah 36 — "None of your people will believe"

The verdict has two halves, and the second is mercy for Nuh himself.

First, the fact: those of his people who were to believe had already believed; no one was to believe after that. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why — their hearts had been sealed with their own obstinacy and contumacy, that is, their stubborn refusal. Nothing was left in them for a message to reach.

Second, the instruction: **"so do not grieve over what they used to do."** Ibn Kathir puts it plainly — do not grieve over them and do not be concerned with their affair. Maʿārif adds that he should now feel free of any concern about their failure to believe.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers a piece of insight here that is worth pausing over. One feels the pinch of sorrow, it says, only when one expects something good to come from someone. Grief is the shadow cast by hope. And then this: *disappointment is not that bad; it has its own relief.* He might as well be disappointed with them. Allah was not hardening His prophet's heart. He was releasing him — telling him he may stop hoping for this particular outcome, and so stop bleeding over it.

That is a delicate mercy, and it is aimed at a very specific kind of pain: the pain of the caller who cannot let go.

## Ayah 37 — "Build the Ark under Our Eyes"

Now the mission turns. Instead of *speak*, the command is *build*.

**"And build the Ark" — wa-iṣnaʿi l-fulk.** Ibn Kathir notes simply that the word *fulk* here means ship.

**"under Our Eyes" — bi-aʿyunina.** Ibn Kathir glosses this: "This means under Our vision." What the phrase *does* for Nuh is unmistakable: he is not working alone or unwatched. Every plank is laid under the vision of the One who commanded the work. Nothing that happens on that building site — including the jeering — escapes Him.

**"and Our revelation" — wa-waḥyinā.** Ibn Kathir: this means, "We will teach you what to do." This is the practical half of the promise. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the obvious human problem: when Nuh was commanded to make an ark, *he knew no ark, nor its making*. So the command came bundled with its own curriculum — in ayah 37, says Maʿārif, he got his first lesson, an orientation to the reality of boat-making. This industry, it adds, the first prototype of the ship-building industry, began at his hands for the first time through divine revelation; what came after is current history.

## What the sources say about the ark itself

Two accounts appear in our sources. Their figures differ — and so do their units — which is itself worth knowing, since neither is Qur'anic text.

Ibn Kathir reports that **Muhammad bin Ishaq** mentioned from the Tawrah: Allah commanded Nuh to make it from Indian oak wood; its length eighty cubits and its width fifty cubits; to coat its interior and exterior with tar and to give it a slanted bow to part the water as it sailed; its height thirty cubits into the sky, in three levels of ten cubits each — the lowest for the animals, both tame and wild, the second for the human beings, the highest for the birds — with its door in the centre and a cover on top that covered the entire ship.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites reports that Jibrīl (peace be upon him) told Nuh (peace be upon him) by means of revelation all about the making of boats, and that the wood used was from the *saul* tree (*shorea robusta*). It then relays historical narratives giving the measurements as three hundred yards long, fifty wide and thirty high — almost a three-storeyed ship — with its ventilators, as was customary, opening to the right and the left.

Treat these as reports about the ark, not as revelation about it. The ayah itself gives no specifications; what it insists on is *who* was teaching.

## The wider point Maʿārif draws: crafts came down with revelation

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān uses this ayah to make a broader claim, and attributes it carefully: it has been reported on the authority of some elders of the early centuries of Islam, in *aṭ-Ṭibb an-Nabawī* of Ḥāfiẓ Shamsud-Dīn adh-Dhahabī, that all industries essential for human beings owe their origin to the process of divine revelation through some prophet, with improvements coming later as needed in different times. The first revelation that came to Adam (peace be upon him), it says, mostly related to the rehabilitation of the land and the establishment of different industries — and the invention of wheeled carts for loading and hauling is part of that chain.

The commentary quotes Sir Syed Ahmad, the founder of the well-known Aligarh College (now the Muslim University of Aligarh, India), who used to say more than a hundred years ago that the world has seen inventions of all sorts in moving vehicles, but its pivot has continued to be the axle and the wheel — the common factor between a bullock-cart, a donkey-cart, rails and cars. So the greatest inventor of moving vehicles is the person who invented the wheel, which is the life and soul of a great many machines. And that invention, Maʿārif adds, unfolded itself at the hands of the first prophet, Adam (peace be upon him), through divine revelation.

The lesson Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws from all this: industries devoted to essential human needs are so important that the blessed prophets have been taught and trained in them through divine revelation. Honest, useful work is not a distraction from a prophetic life. In ayah 37 it *is* the prophetic assignment.

## "Do not address Me concerning those who did wrong"

The second half of ayah 37 is the hardest line in the passage: **"and do not address Me on behalf of those who did wrong; they are surely to be drowned."**

Note who is being restrained. This is the man who used to pray for forgiveness for the people who had just stoned him unconscious. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says it directly: soon after being instructed how he would make an ark, he was told that a flood would come and his people would be drowned, and that at the time he was not to intercede out of compassion on their behalf.

What holds this together is ayah 36, which has already established that no faith remains in them to be salvaged.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then traces what followed. Because arrangements had already been made — as ayah 37 indicates, *they are to be drowned* — it was under these conditions that Nuh uttered the invocation against his people preserved in Sūrah Nūḥ: "My Lord, do not leave upon the earth any inhabitant from among the disbelievers. Indeed, if You were to leave them, they will mislead Your servants and will not procreate anyone but the wicked and disbelieving" (71:26–27). And in answer to that prayer, Maʿārif says, the people of Nuh were drowned en masse. So the announcement came first and the prayer followed it; the drowning that eventually came was the answer to the prayer.

## Ayah 38 — the chiefs come by, and laugh

The mockery was not a single incident. Ibn Kathir's rendering has it as a habit: *as he was constructing the ship, **whenever** the chiefs of his people passed by him, they mocked at him.* Maʿārif frames the whole episode as what went on "during the period he was making the ark" — the total lack of concern his people showed for their own sad end. Not one insult, then, but a routine. The commute past the madman's boat.

And note who was doing it: Ibn Kathir specifies *the chiefs* of his people — the leading men. The opposition was led from the top.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives us the exchange as it went. When the chieftains saw him busy with this project under a divine command, they would ask him, "What are you doing?" He said, "A flood is to come, therefore I am making an ark." And they would mock him and say: *we have no water to drink here, and this wise man is planning to sail in a boat on this dry land.*

Ibn Kathir's summary is that they were teasing him and rejecting his warning that they would drown in the coming flood.

Sit with the position Nuh was in. Every hammer-blow was public, unfinished-looking, and indefensible by any argument available to him. He could not produce the flood on demand. He could only keep building. Obedience here meant looking foolish for as long as the work took — and that is often exactly what obedience costs.

## "If you mock us, we shall mock you"

His reply in ayah 38 needs care, because on its face it looks like a prophet returning insult for insult — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is emphatic that this cannot be what it means. Ridicule, it says, is contrary to the spiritual station of the prophets. It is simply not permissible for anyone; in fact it is *ḥarām*, unlawful. And the Qur'an says: "O those who have believed, no people should mock at other people — maybe they are better than them" (49:11).

So what is meant? Maʿārif reads it as a *pragmatic* response to their mockery: conditions would change and events would unfold in such a manner that they themselves would become the cause of their being mocked at. The sense, in its own words, is like saying: "when you are seized by the punishment, we shall be telling you that this was the outcome of your mockery."

Ibn Kathir reads the same line as **a severe threat and a serious warning** — not banter, but a sentence being read out.

There is a lesson buried in this for anyone quick with a comeback. Even when he was in the right, even when the reversal was certain, the prophet's words are read by these scholars as warning rather than ridicule returned. What is coming to the mockers is announced; it is not relished.

## Ayah 39 — "You will soon know"

The passage ends on *soon*: "You will soon come to know." The argument is not settled by debate. It is left to be settled by events.

And the knowledge promised is a *sorting*: you will come to know **who** it is on whom a torment comes that covers him with disgrace, and on whom a lasting torment falls. The very question the chiefs thought they had answered — which side here is the ridiculous one — is the question that will be answered *to* them.

Two punishments are named, and both Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān read them the same way:

- **ʿadhābun yukhzīhi** — a torment that covers him with disgrace. Ibn Kathir: this means it will humiliate him *in this life*. Maʿārif: the punishment of the mortal world — and the worldly punishment Allah had told Nuh He would send against these people was the flood. Note the word chosen: not merely pain, but *disgrace*. Men who built their lives on standing among their people are answered in the currency they cared about.
- **ʿadhābun muqīm** — a lasting torment. Ibn Kathir: continuous and everlasting. Maʿārif: the never-ending punishment of the Hereafter.

The first is the punishment that arrives; the second is the punishment that stays.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān tells how it fell. Nuh made the ark as he was ordered. When the initial signs of the flood came before them — water beginning to overflow from the earth — he was commanded to embark along with his family and the few believers who had believed in him, loading a pair each of the animals that serve human needs: cow, ox, goat, horse, mule. He put everyone on the ark as ordered. And the believers who boarded with him, after all those years of calling, were only a few.

## Living it

- **You are allowed to stop grieving.** Ayah 36 is permission from Allah Himself to a caller who has done everything: do not grieve over them, do not be concerned with their affair. Sorrow is felt where good is still expected; where that expectation is honestly finished, the sorrow may be laid down.
- **Build while they laugh.** Nuh could not produce the flood to order; he could only keep working. Obedience often looks unreasonable for the entire stretch between the command and the vindication.
- **Work under His vision, not theirs.** "Build the Ark under Our Eyes" — under Our vision, says Ibn Kathir — reframes the whole scene. The audience that matters is watching already.
- **Take the teaching with the task.** The command came with *wa-waḥyinā* — "We will teach you what to do." He was told to make something he had never seen, and taught how in the same breath.
- **Do not answer mockery with mockery.** These scholars would not even let a prophet's line in ayah 38 be read as ridicule, given 49:11 and the station of the prophets. Warn if you must; do not sneer.
- **Let "soon" do the arguing.** Ayah 39 hands the verdict to time and to Allah. That is a restful place for a believer to stand.

passages.title: The Flood: boarding, the drowning son, the receding waters
passages.tafsir:
Ayat 40–44 carry the story of the Flood at its sharpest point: the waters are released, the ark is loaded and boarded, a father loses a son mid-conversation, and the waters are called back. One question runs through all five verses — **who is protected, and by what?** A ship, a mountain, a bloodline: the passage tests each and leaves standing only the mercy of Allah.

## Ayah 40: the sign was an oven

*"At last, when Our command came and the oven overflowed."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān marks this verse as the point where the description of the flood begins. The commentators spent real effort on the trigger: **التنور (tannūr)**.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the word carries more than one sense in Arabic. The floor of the earth is called a *tannūr*; the oven that bakes bread is a *tannūr*; a raised part of the land is also called *tannūr*. From that, three readings developed:

- **The surface of the land**, from which the water started overflowing. Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn ʿAbbas that *at-tannūr* is the face of the earth — meaning the face of the earth became gushing water springs, and this continued until water gushed forth from the *tanānīr*, the places of fire. Ibn Kathir says this is the opinion of the majority of the Salaf (the earliest generations) and of the scholars of the Khalaf (the later ones).
- **The oven of Adam** (peace be upon him), said to have been at ʿAynul-Wardah in Syria, from which the water overflowed.
- **Nuh's own oven**, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān locates in Kufah, noting that most commentators — al-Ḥasan, Mujahid, al-Shaʿbi, ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbas and others — went by this view.

Al-Qurtubi, quoted in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, dissolves the disagreement: the sayings of the commentators only *appear* to differ. When the water began to bulge out, it overflowed from the bread-baking oven, and from the surface of the land, and from the oven of ʿAynul-Wardah in Syria — all of it. The Qur'an itself states both directions of water in Surah al-Qamar: *"Then We opened the gates of the heaven with rain pouring down and caused the earth to burst out with springs"* (54:11).

**Why an oven, of all things?** Ibn ʿAbbas says that Allah had told Nuh (peace be upon him): *when you see water overflowing from the oven in your home, know that the flood has come* (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Qurtubi and Mazhari). The sign was not thunder over the horizon but water rising in the hearth — the driest, hottest, most domestic corner of a house. When the command of Allah comes, the settled properties of things do not argue.

## Ayah 40: what was loaded, and who

**"A pair of two from every kind."** Ibn Kathir says Allah commanded Nuh (peace be upon him) to select one pair from every kind of creature possessing a soul and load them on the ship; some said this included other creatures as well, such as pairs of plants, male and female. He also passes on the report that the first of the birds to enter the ship was the parrot, and the last of the animals to enter was the donkey. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a clarifying limit: what was loaded were animals born to a pair of male and female that cannot survive in water. All sea life is therefore excluded, and so are land-based life forms that come into being without male-female conjunction; what is left is essentially the domestic animals — the cow, the ox, the water buffalo, the goat and their like.

**"And your family — except him against whom the Word has already gone forth."** Ibn Kathir explains this as the members of his household and his relatives, except those who did not believe in Allah: among them the son of Nuh, Yam, and the wife of Nuh, who was a disbeliever in Allah and His Messenger. Prophethood does not make a household immune. The exception is placed inside the rescue order itself, so that the ark is defined from the first moment by faith rather than by lineage.

**"And those who believe."** Then the quiet, devastating comment: *"And none believed with him, except a few."* Ibn Kathir underlines what "a few" means here — only a very small number believed, and that after the long period Nuh (peace be upon him) spent among them: nine hundred and fifty years. He reports from Ibn ʿAbbas that "they were eighty people including their women." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the exact number has not been determined in the Qur'an and Hadith, and gives the same report from Ibn ʿAbbas: eighty in total, including three sons of Nuh (peace be upon him) — Sam, Ham and Yafith — and their three wives; the fourth son stayed with the disbelievers and was drowned with them.

Nine and a half centuries of calling; eighty souls. If you have ever measured your own worth by the response you get, this ayah is for you.

## Ayah 41: "With the name of Allah it sails and anchors"

*"Embark therein: in the Name of Allah will be its course and its anchorage."*

**The two words.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains *majrā* as sailing or moving, and *mursā* as stopping or anchoring; the sense is that the moving of this conveyance owes itself to the power of Allah and is with His name alone, as does its stopping, which is subservient to nothing but His power. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also notes the pronunciation: in the reading (*qirāʾah*, a transmitted way of reciting) of Imam Ḥafṣ it is read *majray*, with a fatḥah on the *mīm* and a major *imālah* — an inclination, a tilting of the vowel sound — on the *rāʾ*. Ibn Kathir records that Abu Rajaʾ al-ʿUtaridi recited it as *mujrīhā wa mursīhā*: "in the Name of Allah, Who will be the One Who moves its course, and rests its anchor."

**Why both halves?** Because, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, a shallow view of things leads a man to assume that he is the one who manufactured the thing and made it move — while the reality lies elsewhere. Man has not created the iron, wood, brass or aluminium that go into these conveyances. Who gave him the intelligence to design and produce all those mechanical parts? Did he create his own intelligence? And the power that hauls tons of weight — petrol, gas, hydro-electricity, water, oxygen, hydrogen — did man create any of it?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then observes that inventing things and making them work makes inventors self-centred: they start living in a hall of mirrors, congratulating themselves until they lose touch with the reality of things on a canvas larger than what they invent. *Bismillāhi majrāhā wa mursāhā* is what Allah tells them through His prophets — in its words, "a key to a door": once a man enters it, he lives in this mortal world but turns into a citizen of the spiritual universe, seeing the beauty of his Lord everywhere in it. From here unfolds the difference between the world of a believer and the world of a disbeliever. But when the believer steps in, the conveyance does not merely shorten his travelling distance — it introduces him to the One higher and more sublime.

**Living it.** Ibn Kathir draws the practical ruling straight from this ayah: it is preferred to mention the Name of Allah at the beginning of all affairs, and the Name of Allah should be mentioned when boarding a ship or when mounting an animal. He cites the parallel instruction in Surah al-Mu'minun — *"And when you have embarked on the ship, you and whoever is with you, then say: All the praises and thanks are to Allah, Who has saved us from the people who are wrongdoers. And say: My Lord! Cause me to land at a blessed landing place, for You are the Best of those who bring to land"* (23:28–29) — and the ayat of Surah az-Zukhruf about the ships and cattle appointed for us to ride (43:12–13). Ibn Kathir notes that this practice has been encouraged in the Sunnah. Your car, your train, your flight: the ayah is not archaeology.

**"Surely, my Lord is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."** A whole civilisation is about to drown, and Nuh (peace be upon him) names his Lord as *Ghafūr, Raḥīm*. Ibn Kathir says precisely that such a statement is suitable while mentioning Allah's vengeance upon the disbelievers by drowning all of them — and he places it alongside *"Surely, your Lord is swift in retribution, and certainly He is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful"* (7:167) and *"But verily, your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind in spite of their wrongdoing. And verily, your Lord is also severe in punishment"* (13:6). The believer's picture of his Lord is not built out of one attribute at a time.

## Ayat 42–43: the son who chose a mountain

*"So it sailed with them amidst waves like mountains."* Ibn Kathir describes water that had completely covered the earth until it encompassed the tops of the mountains and even rose over them by fifteen cubits; it was also said that the waves rose over the mountains by a height of eighty miles. Ibn Kathir's point is the contrast: through all of that, this one ship continued to move upon the water, sailing by the permission of Allah — under His shade, His help, His protection and His blessing, as Allah says elsewhere, *"floating under Our Eyes: a reward for him who had been rejected"* (54:14).

Ibn Kathir identifies the son as the fourth son of Nuh, named Yam, a disbeliever; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the name as Kinʿān (Canaan). The verse describes him as one "who had separated himself apart," and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says he was already in league with those disbelieving enemies. Ibn Kathir says his father called him at the time of boarding the ship, that he might believe and embark with them, and so be saved from drowning like the other disbelievers.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the scene with great tenderness. The call was made out of Nuh's paternal compassion. In all likelihood, it says, Nuh (peace be upon him) did not know that his son was a disbeliever; and even if he did know, the good counsel he gave was in the spirit of asking him to repent from disbelief and enter the fold of faith. That is what *"O my son! Embark with us and be not with the disbelievers"* (ayah 42) is: a call to repent, in the last available second.

**The son's answer is the most human sentence in the passage.** *"I will betake myself to some mountain, it will save me from the water"* (ayah 43). Ibn Kathir says he believed, in his ignorance, that the flood would not reach the tops of the mountains and that if he clung to a summit he would be saved from drowning. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it as a man treating the flood as something that would pass away, telling his father not to worry about him. He did not deny that danger was coming. He simply had his own plan for it. Notice, too, what he refuses: he is offered a ship whose sailing and anchoring have been placed in the Name of Allah, and he prefers rock. Every generation has its mountains — wealth, position, cleverness, a strong body, a safe country.

**The father's reply is the heart of the whole passage:** *"This day there is no savior from the decree of Allah except him on whom He has mercy"* (ayah 43). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: nothing was going to save anyone, not even a mountain, from the punishment of Allah on that day, and there was no way one could remain safe from it unless Allah Himself were to show mercy. Note that not even the ark is named here as the savior. The ark is where the mercy was; the mercy is what saves.

*"And waves came in between them, so he was among the drowned."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this father-son dialogue was going on from a distance when a wave of the flood rose and took him down and away. The conversation does not conclude. It is interrupted.

## Ayah 44: the water is called back

*"O earth! Swallow up your water, and O sky! Withhold your rain."* Ibn Kathir: when the people of the earth were all drowned except for the people on the ship, Allah commanded the earth to swallow its water, which had sprung from it and gathered upon it, and then commanded the sky to cease raining. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Tafsir Qurtubi and Mazhari) adds the mercy folded into the recession: the water that had bulged out from the earth was to be taken back in by the earth, and the rainwater that had already accumulated on the ground was channelled into rivers and streams for human beings to benefit by it. The punishment is drained; what remains becomes provision.

**Being addressed at all.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the question of why Allah gives His commands by addressing the heaven and the earth, when outwardly these are not sentient entities. Some commentators have taken it in a figurative sense. But it holds that things which appear non-conscious and lifeless to *our* perception are in reality live and conscious — though their consciousness is not of the level given to humankind, which is why, being counted as inanimate, they were not obligated with the precepts and injunctions of the Sharīʿah (the sacred law). It cites *"and there is no such thing which does not glorify Him with praises"* (17:44) — and glorification depends on knowing Allah, and knowing depends on reason and consciousness — together with *"gave each thing its form, then guided it"* (20:50). Everything recognises its Creator and whatever task He has assigned it, and keeps doing it staunchly as due. The commentary quotes the couplet of Rumi: dust, air, water and fire are all servants — for you and me, dead; with Him, alive.

**"And the decree was fulfilled."** Ibn Kathir: all of those who disbelieved in Allah were removed from the people of the earth; not a single one of them remained upon it.

**"And it rested on Mount Jūdī."** Mujahid, as reported by Ibn Kathir: Jūdī is a mountain in al-Jazīrah (northwest Mesopotamia). On the day of the drowning the mountains sought to tower above each other, each striving to be higher so as not to be overcome by the water. But this mountain humbled itself for Allah, the Mighty and Sublime, and therefore it was not drowned — and this is why Nuh's ship anchored upon it. The son sought a mountain that would rise; the ark landed on the mountain that lowered itself.

Qatadah, also via Ibn Kathir, adds that the ship rested upon Mount Jūdī for a month before the people came down from it, and that Allah made Nuh's ship remain there as a lesson and a sign — the early generations of this Ummah, this community, even saw it. Ibn Kathir remarks: how many ships are there that have come after it and have been destroyed and became dust? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that Mount Jūdiyy still stands there by that name, located on the border of Armenia near Ibn ʿUmar Island, north of Mosul in Iraq. It is a mountain range, part of which is called Jūdiyy and another part known as Ararat; the present Torah identifies the resting place as Mount Ararat, so there is not much of a contradiction between these two reports. These accounts mention as well that pieces of the ark are still at many places in Iraq, kept and used as a relic.

**"Away with the people who are wrongdoing!"** Ibn Kathir explains this as destruction and loss for them, and says the term "away with" here implies being far away from the mercy of Allah — for they were destroyed to the last of them, and none of them survived. Read against ayah 43, it is exact: the only thing that saved anyone was mercy, and these are the people put far from it.

## The voyage and the fast of ʿĀshūrāʾ

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmits from Tafsir at-Tabari and al-Baghawi a timeline: Nuh (peace be upon him) embarked the ark on the tenth of Rajab; for six months the ark sailed on the waters of the flood; when it reached the spot where the Baytullah — the House of Allah — stood, it made seven circuits, Allah having raised His House higher from being submerged; and then, on the tenth of Muḥarram, the day of ʿĀshūrāʾ, the flood subsided and the ark came to rest at Mount Jūdiyy. Nuh (peace be upon him) observed a thanksgiving fast on that day and asked everyone on the ark to do the same — and some reports say that even the animals that had shared the ark fasted on that day (Mazhari and Qurtubi).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the importance of ʿĀshūrāʾ has been recognised in all the religious codes of the blessed prophets, and that in early Islam — before the fasts of Ramadan became obligatory — fasting on ʿĀshūrāʾ was farḍ, that is, obligatory. It is no longer farḍ, but it continues to be a practice of the prophets and a source of reward forever. The first response of a rescued man was not celebration. It was hunger, deliberately chosen, in gratitude.

## What the passage asks of us

Read as a unit, ayat 40–44 take away one false shelter after another. **Property and habit**: the sign of the flood came up out of the household oven, and water poured from the very places built to hold fire (ayah 40). **Lineage**: a prophet's son and a prophet's wife are excluded by the very clause that carries the believers aboard (ayah 40). **Self-reliance**: the boarding word is not "we sail" but "in the Name of Allah will be its course and its anchorage" (ayah 41). **Nature's strength**: the mountains that reared up were overcome; the mountain that humbled itself for Allah carried the ark (ayat 43–44).

What is left standing is the one thing the passage says out loud: *"except him on whom He has mercy."* So board while boarding is open — take the Name of Allah on your going out and your coming home, keep calling the people you love even when they are not listening, and do not mistake the plank you are standing on for the One who holds it up.

passages.title: Noah pleads for his son and disembarks
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat close the account of Nuh (peace be upon him) and the flood, and they turn on a single word. Back in ayah 40, Allah had promised to save Nuh's *family*. Here a father stands with the water around his son and asks for that promise to be honoured — and is told that the word does not mean what he took it to mean. Everything else follows from that correction: the rebuke, the repentance, the command to come down the mountain, and finally the peace spoken over a circle of people far wider than one household. By the end, the question "who counts as your family?" has been answered twice — once by exclusion, once by inclusion.

## The plea, and the promise it rests on

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene. Canaan, the son of Nuh (peace be upon him), did not board the ark despite his father's counsel and call. His father was still caught up emotionally as he watched his son surrounded by the waves of the flood, and his filial love, in Maʿārif's phrase, "knocked at another door" — he turned to his Lord. The only court of appeal left was the court of the Most Just of judges, since everything was in His power and control and He could still save the boy.

Notice *how* he prays. He does not simply ask; he argues from what Allah Himself has said. Ibn Kathir gives the sense of "my son is of my family" as: *You promised to save my family and Your promise is the truth that does not fail — how then can he be drowned, when You are the Most Just of the judges?* That is a prophet's way of asking.

Ibn Kathir also tells us what kind of speech this is: **a request for information and an inquiry** from Nuh concerning the circumstances of his son's drowning.

## The answer: the circle was never drawn by blood

The reply comes with his name in it — "O Nuh!" — and it is stern. Ibn Kathir explains "he is not of your family" as: *he is not among those whom I promised to save; I only promised you that I would save those of your family who believe.* And he sends the reader back to the original promise: **"and your family except him against whom the Word has already gone forth"** (11:40). For his son, Ibn Kathir says, it had already been decreed that he would be drowned, due to his disbelief and his opposition to his father, the Prophet of Allah.

So the sentence is not a denial of biology. ʿAbdur-Razzāq recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās said of him: **"He was the son of Nuh, but he opposed him in deeds and intention."** The blood is real. What is denied is that blood puts him inside the circle of the promise.

Three comments in the sources all point at conduct. Ibn Kathir's text renders the next clause of the ayah as **"verily, his work is unrighteous."** ʿIkrimah said that in some of the modes of recitation the wording here is *innahu ʿamila ʿamalan ghayra ṣāliḥ* — "verily, he worked deeds that were not righteous." And Maʿārif summarises the whole rebuke this way: the son was no longer part of his family *because he was not good and right in what he did*. Deeds and intention, not descent.

## What kinship cannot do — and what it does not forbid

Maʿārif draws a religious ruling straight out of this: a believer and a disbeliever may be blood relatives, but when it comes to religious and collective matters, that kinship has no effect. A person may be high born, from the progeny of men of high spiritual status — one may even have the honour of being among the progeny of our most noble Prophet ﷺ — and this high lineage and prophetic connection will still not be taken into consideration in religious matters if the person is not a believer. "In religion, everything functionally depends on faith, goodness and the fear of Allah. One who is good in deeds and fears Allah, he is ours. If not like that, he is an alien."

The proof Maʿārif offers is history. Had concessions based on kinship been given in religious matters, brothers would not have crossed swords against each other in the battlefields of Badr and Uhud. Badr, Uhud and al-Aḥzāb were fought among individuals coming from the same families. So Islamic brotherhood does not hinge on lineal bond, or on geographical or linguistic unity; it revolves around faith and deed — which is what **"The believers are but brothers"** (49:10) means. And the Qurʼan makes the reverse side of it starker still through the words of Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him): **"Indeed, we have nothing to do with you and with whatever you worship other than Allah"** (60:4).

**The qualification matters as much as the rule.** Maʿārif deliberately restricts all of this to *religious* matters. In worldly dealings, demonstrating good social behaviour, moral grace, favour and generosity is something else entirely: it is quite permissible to deal even with someone not good in these ways — in fact it is recommended, and an act worthy of reward. The countless instances in which the Prophet ﷺ and his noble Companions treated non-Muslims with compassion, favour and good grace are enough to prove it. So the wall runs through religious loyalty, not through kindness.

Maʿārif then turns the same principle on our own time: raising the edifice of nationality on homeland, language or colour, so that Muslims are segregated into one or another "nation" under false banners, is contrary to the Qurʼan and the Sunnah.

## "Ask not of Me that of which you have no knowledge"

First, what Nuh (peace be upon him) knew. Maʿārif's reading is that he did not know about his son's disbelief clearly and fully; he thought his son a hypocrite, and so still took him to be a believer. That is why he identified him as part of "my family" and prayed for his rescue. Had he known the true state of affairs, he would not have made such a prayer — because he had already been instructed in clear terms, in ayah 37, that once the flood came he was not to speak to Allah about those who had crossed the limit. After an injunction that clear, Maʿārif says, it was not possible for a prophet of Allah to venture something against it. Maʿārif then cites the author of *Bayān al-Qurʼān* for the only likely explanation: the desired objective of the prayer was that his son become a believer, not that he be saved from the flood in the condition he was in.

And yet — this is the point Maʿārif refuses to soften — Allah did not take Nuh's lack of knowledge, nor a prayer built on it, as sound excuses. He was questioned as to why he would make such a prayer at all. Maʿārif calls this a slip at the highest level of the station of a prophet, and adds that Nuh (peace be upon him) will himself refer to it on the Day of Resurrection, when the whole creation comes asking him to intercede with the Lord on their behalf: he will excuse himself by mentioning what happened to him here, and will not dare any intercession. One request, made out of a father's love, and a prophet still recalls it on the Last Day.

**The rule that follows.** Maʿārif states it plainly: one should first find out whether the objective he is praying for is permissible and lawful. It is prohibited to make duʿāʼ — supplication, asking Allah — under doubtful circumstances. Tafsir *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī*, with reference to al-Bayḍāwī, notes that since this verse tells us of the prohibition of duʿāʼ under *doubtful* circumstances, it is automatically inferred that praying for anything known to be impermissible and unlawful is all the more prohibited.

Maʿārif then applies this to a familiar scene: shaykhs used to raising their hands in prayer for anyone who walks in asking, when most of the time they know the person is not in the right, or is unjust, in the very matter he wants prayed for — or is seeking an office through which he will earn unlawfully or usurp someone's right. Where the attending circumstances are known, such prayers are unlawful and impermissible. Even where the circumstances are merely doubtful, taking the initiative to make duʿāʼ before getting to know the circumstances as they are is still not appropriate.

**And then the response.** Allah says: *"so ask not of Me that of which you have no knowledge!"* Nuh says: *"I seek refuge with You from asking You that of which I have no knowledge."* He takes the very words back into his mouth. Maʿārif calls ayah 47 an apology: in gist, a return to Allah in submission and entreaty — a prayer for the protection of Allah, His forgiveness for past omissions, and a request for His mercy. Then the closing clause: "And unless You forgive me and have mercy on me, I would indeed be one of the losers." A prophet, after a single question, places himself entirely at the mercy of Allah and reckons that without it he is ruined.

Maʿārif draws the practical lesson: should a person commit a mistake, let him not rely on his personal resolve to stay safe from it in future.
